messages.subject: Re: Position of xlabel
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The problem with that suggestion is that the OP wants to use an
expression for the x label and \n doesn't work in expressions. The \n
trick on y should work as long as the font size isn't altered, but try
this for the expression (borrowed from memory by a trick I saw on
R-help for this kind of thing):

scale_x_continuous(expression(atop(phantom(0),
                              paste("application execution time[",mu,"s]"))),
                   limits=c(0,125))

atop basically creates the space for a fraction without the line.
phantom(0) creates space for the 0 character but doesn't print it.  A
little bit more than a line of space is added, but it does give
separation :)

Someone gave a better, more robust solution for the spacing problem in
this forum a month or two ago that adjusts for changes in font size,
etc., but I can't find it in the archives at the moment.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I have this in my .Rprofile, until the next ggplot2 update (I think it
was Koshke who posted it),

require(ggplot2)

guide_axis <- function(at, labels, position="right", theme) {
  position <- match.arg(position, c("top", "bottom", "right", "left"))
  at <- unit(at, "native")
  length <- theme$axis.ticks.length
  label_pos <- length + theme$axis.ticks.margin
  one <- unit(1, "npc")
  label_render <- switch(position,
    top = , bottom = "axis.text.x",
    left = , right = "axis.text.y"
  )
  label_x <- switch(position,
    top = ,
    bottom = at,
    right = label_pos,
    left = one - label_pos
  )
  label_y <- switch(position,
    top = label_pos,
    bottom = one - label_pos,
    right = ,
    left = at,
  )
  if (is.list(labels)) {
    if (any(sapply(labels, is.language))) {
      labels <- do.call(expression, labels)
    } else {
      labels <- unlist(labels)
    }
  }
  labels <- theme_render(theme, label_render, labels, label_x, label_y)
  line <- switch(position,
    top =    theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 0, 1, 0),
    bottom = theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 1, 1, 1),
    right =  theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 0, 1, 0, 1),
    left =   theme_render(theme, "axis.line", 1, 0, 1, 1)
  )
  ticks <- switch(position,
    top =    theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", at, 0, at, length),
    bottom = theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", at, one - length, at, 1),
    right =  theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", 0, at, length, at),
    left =   theme_render(theme, "axis.ticks", one - length, at, 1, at)
  )
  absoluteGrob(
    gList(ticks, labels, line),
    width = grobWidth(labels) + label_pos,
    height = grobHeight(labels) + label_pos
  )
}

utils::assignInNamespace("guide_axis",guide_axis, "ggplot2")

Hi @all

Sometimes it is really frustrating to work with R as a novice
especially when one wants to change simple things and even after a

I have the following simple dotplot graph:

nutrients
p <- ggplot(nutrients, aes(x=diss_N, y=d15N))

p+geom_point(aes(shape=factor(Catchment)), size=3)  + theme_bw() +
opts(legend.key=theme_rect(fill=NULL,colour="white")) +
opts(legend.position = "bottom")  + xlab(expression(paste('DIN (mg',~
L^{-1},')'))) + ylab(expression(paste(delta^{15},'N (DIN)'~'(\u2030
AIR)')))   + opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size=13), axis.text.y =
theme_text(size=13, hjust = 0.8), legend.title = theme_text(size=15),
legend.text = theme_text(size=15), axis.title.x = theme_text(size=15),
axis.title.y = theme_text(size=15, angle = 90)) + opts(legend.position
= c(0.9, 0.9))+ opts(legend.background=theme_rect(col = "black")) +
scale_shape("Catchments")

I think most of the journals don't like the grey grid lines so I just
want to have them in black. However, none of the following additions
did it:

+ opts(panel.background = theme_rect(colour = black))
+ opts(axis.line = theme_segment(colour = "black")) this only changed

the graph.

Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
Martin

B

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm not sure whether you want all plots on the same page or each in
its own page.
In either case I'd start by melting the data.frame into long format.

library(ggplot2)

d = data.frame(id = seq(1, 100), matrix(rnorm(100 * 5), ncol = 5))

m = melt(d, id="id")

plotone = function(.d) qplot(id, value, data=.d, geom="line")

pdf("one.pdf")
qplot(id, value, data=m, geom="line") + facet_wrap(~variable, ncol=1)
dev.off()

pdf("multiple.pdf")
d_ply(m, .(variable), plotone, .print=TRUE)
dev.off()

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: barchart with proportion or percent rather than count
messages.subject_clean: barchart with proportion or percent rather than count
messages.body_plain:
Suppose we have a factor (a nominal variable) and we want to plot its distribution with a barplot. The code for plotting the counts (or frequencies) is straightforward in ggplot2. But how does one relabel the quantitative axis (the "continuous scale") for proportions or percents? That is, how does one make a barplot of proportions rather than counts?

In this email I show one way. But it requires the user to hard-code two things:

(1) a formula for the percent or proportion

(2) a non-default name for the y axis.

Is there a simpler or more elegant (and less error-prone) approach?

set.seed(1)
NN<-12
categories<- c("dog", "flea", "human", "rat", NA)
DAAT<-data.frame(
 	species=factor(sample(categories , prob=c( 1.5 ,3, 1,8,1), size=NN, replace=T), levels=categories)
)
print(DAAT)
#	Order the bars by frequency:
DAAT$species<- factor( DAAT$species, levels=rev(names(sort(table( DAAT$species)))))
print(summary(DAAT))
require(ggplot2)
#	A barplot of frequencies or counts is straightforward:
print(
 	ggplot(data=DAAT, aes(x=species)) + geom_bar()
)
#	Here is a hard-coded solution to put proportion on the y axis.
print(
 	ggplot(data=DAAT, aes(x=species, weight=1/nrow(DAAT))) + geom_bar()
#	Without the following, the y axis will be incorrectly labeled "count".
 		+ scale_y_continuous(name="Proportion ")
)

Thanks for any comments

Jacob A. Wegelin
Assistant Professor
Department of Biostatistics
Virginia Commonwealth University
730 East Broad Street Room 3006
P. O. Box 980032
Richmond VA 23298-0032

messages.subject: Re: Plot 95%CI with lines, not shading ()
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

How about something like this?

x <- 1:10
dd <- data.frame(x = x, y = 0.8 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(10, s = 1.5))

m <- lm(y ~ x, data = dd)
pp <- data.frame(x = x, predict(m, interval = 'confidence')

g <- ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
       geom_smooth(method = 'lm', size = 1, se = FALSE)
g + geom_smooth(data = pp, aes(y = lwr), color = 'dodgerblue') +
    geom_smooth(data = pp, aes(y = upr), color = 'dodgerblue')

HTH,
Dennis

On Monday, May 2, 2011 at 8:44 PM, Jacob Wegelin wrote:

>
> Suppose we have a factor (a nominal variable) and we want to plot its distribution with a barplot. The code for plotting the counts (or frequencies) is straightforward in ggplot2. But how does one relabel the quantitative axis (the "continuous scale") for proportions or percents? That is, how does one make a barplot of proportions rather than counts?
>
> In this email I show one way. But it requires the user to hard-code two things:
>
> (1) a formula for the percent or proportion
>
> (2) a non-default name for the y axis.
>
> Is there a simpler or more elegant (and less error-prone) approach?
>
> set.seed(1)
> NN<-12
> categories<- c("dog", "flea", "human", "rat", NA)
> DAAT<-data.frame(
> species=factor(sample(categories , prob=c( 1.5 ,3, 1,8,1), size=NN, replace=T), levels=categories)
> )
> print(DAAT)
> # Order the bars by frequency:
> DAAT$species<- factor( DAAT$species, levels=rev(names(sort(table( DAAT$species)))))
> print(summary(DAAT))
> require(ggplot2)
> # A barplot of frequencies or counts is straightforward:
> print(
> ggplot(data=DAAT, aes(x=species)) + geom_bar()
> )
> # Here is a hard-coded solution to put proportion on the y axis.
> print(
> ggplot(data=DAAT, aes(x=species, weight=1/nrow(DAAT))) + geom_bar()
> # Without the following, the y axis will be incorrectly labeled "count".
> + scale_y_continuous(name="Proportion ")
> )
>
> Thanks for any comments
>
> Jacob A. Wegelin

Here is another solution.

x <- 1:10
dd <- data.frame(x = x, y = 0.8 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(10, s = 1.5))

ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + stat_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red", geom = "ribbon", fill = NA)

#some tweaking to get rid to the vertical lines of the ribbon. The trick: expand the range with scale() then zoom in with coord()
ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + stat_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red", geom = "ribbon", fill = NA, fullrange = TRUE) + scale_x_continuous(limits = diff(range(dd$x)) * c(-0.2, 0.2) + range(dd$x)) + coord_cartesian(xlim = range(pretty(dd$x)))

Best regards,

Thierry

messages.body_plain:
So here's my lazy solution:

xrange<- function(x, margin){
r<-range(x, na.rm=TRUE)
d<-diff(r)
m<-c(d*-margin, d*margin)
return (r+m)
}

where x is the x-data to be plotted, and margin is a decimal of how
much 'margin' we want around the x-data so that we dont get points
lying on the boundaries of the plot area. eg 0.05 is a 5% margin above
and below

then we modify Thierry's command:

ggplot(dd, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method =
"lm", se = FALSE) + stat_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "red", geom =
"ribbon", fill = NA, fullrange = TRUE) + scale_x_continuous(limits =

xrange(x, 0.2) + coord_cartesian(xlim = xrange(x,0.05))

just posting it here so that someone else can use benefit

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for this solution. Your numbers are different because I divided by the number of rows, whereas with your syntax, ggplot2 does not count the NA row(s) in the sample size. The following produces a plot identical to yours: set.seed(1) NN<-12 categories<- c("dog", "flea", "human", "rat", NA) DAAT<-data.frame( species=factor(sample(categories , prob=c( 1.5 ,3, 1,8,1) , size=NN, replace=T) , levels=categories) ) # Order the bars by frequency: DAAT$species<- factor( DAAT$species, levels=rev(names(sort(table( DAAT$species))))) print( ggplot(data=DAAT, aes(x=species, weight=1/sum(!is.na (DAAT$species)))) + geom_bar() + scale_y_continuous(name="Proportion ") ) Your syntax translated into the intermediate syntax (halfway between the black box of qplot and the explicit syntax of layer), with bar (as you sugggested) instead of histogram, is: ggplot(data=DAAT, aes(x=species, y=..density.., group=1)) + geom_bar() + scale_y_continuous(name="Proportion") and the full layer syntax is: ggplot() + layer(data=DAAT, mapping=aes(x=species, y=..density.., group=1), geom="bar") + scale_y_continuous(name="Proportion") The crux is the mysterious "group" term. Without that term, all bars are of equal height. The help page online for geom_bar says: “Layers are divided into groups by the group aesthetic. By default this is set to the interaction of all categorical variables present in the plot.” Has anyone found an explanation of what it means for layers to be divided into groups in this context? messages.subject_clean: defining the order of data when plotted
messages.body_plain:
Hi
I am creating a bar plot and I would like to retain the order of the
data in the data frame (along the x-axis and the order of the counts
for the y-axis).  The data frame contains presummarised data.  In the
example below, I would like to keep the order of the people (person)
for the x-axis as it is in the data frame along with the chronological
order of the day.  Currently, the data is ordered alphabetically, yet
I have been able to order the days in chronological order using the
'group' option within the aes portion of ggplot.

I have found several posts that indicate the use of 'relevel',
'reorder', or 'factor' but have not been able to determine how to use
these functions correctly.

Any help or suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you
Emilio

Example:
library(ggplot2)
steve <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
amy <- c(2,3,4,5,6,1)
mike <- c(3,4,5,6,1,2)
becky <- c(4,5,6,1,2,3)

data <- data.frame()
data <- rbind(steve, amy, mike, becky)
colnames(data) <- c("mon", "tues", "wed", "thur", "fri", "sat")

TdataM <- melt(t(data))
colname(TdataM) <- c("day", "person", "count")

g <- ggplot(TdataM, aes(person, count, fill=day,
group=interaction("mon", "tues", "wed", "thur", "fri", "sat")))
g <- g + geom_bar(position="stack", stat="identity")
g <- g + scale_fill_discrete(breaks=c("mon", "tues", "wed", "thur",
"fri", "sat"))
g

messages.subject: Re: defining the order of data when plotted

messages.body_plain:
Emilio,
I would just change the order of the levels. Reorder only works when you have another continuous variable to order the levels.

library(ggplot2)
steve <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
amy <- c(2,3,4,5,6,1)
mike <- c(3,4,5,6,1,2)
becky <- c(4,5,6,1,2,3)

data <- data.frame()
data <- rbind(steve, amy, mike, becky)
colnames(data) <- c("mon", "tues", "wed", "thur", "fri", "sat")

TdataM <- melt(t(data))

colnames(TdataM) <- c("day", "person", "count")
TdataM$person <- factor(TdataM$person, levels = c("steve", "amy", "mike", "becky"))
TdataM$day <- factor(TdataM$day, levels = c("mon", "tues", "wed", "thur", "fri", "sat"))

g <- ggplot(TdataM, aes(person, count, fill=day))

g <- g + geom_bar(position="stack", stat="identity")

g <- g + scale_fill_discrete()

Luciano

messages.subject_clean: control color in stacked barplot; make it grayscale
messages.body_plain:
A simple reproducible example is below these two questions.

(1) How could I with a single, simple command make everything in a particular plot black and white, or grayscale?

I do not want to set all the plots in the current R session to grayscale, just a particular plot.

(2) How could I assign three colors of my choice in a particular plot, something like the following base graphics command?

col=c("gray", "white", "gray")

Example: We want to make a stacked barplot from the following dataframe.

TINYDATA<-data.frame( diagnosis=c("A", "B", "C"), FREQ=c(5,9, 1))

require(ggplot2)

#	The following makes a single black bar with the groups indistinguishable.
print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis)) + geom_bar())

#	The following assigns a different, seemingly arbitrary color to each diagnosis group:
print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=diagnosis)) + geom_bar())

#	Curiously, the following does not change the bars to black and white. Instead
#	it eliminates the gray background of the grid inside the plot:
print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=diagnosis)) + geom_bar() + theme_bw()  )

#	The following also produces a brightly colored plot, surprisingly:
print(
 	ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=diagnosis)) + geom_bar()
 		+ scale_colour_manual(values=c("gray", "black", "white"))
)

#	The following makes a two-color plot and labels these colors "black" and "white" in a legend:
print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=c("black", "white", "black"))) + geom_bar() )

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob -

> # The following makes a single black bar with the groups indistinguishable.
> print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis)) + geom_bar())
>
> # The following assigns a different, seemingly arbitrary color to each diagnosis group:
> print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=diagnosis)) + geom_bar())

These are the default colors in a categorical color scale.

> # Curiously, the following does not change the bars to black and white. Instead
> # it eliminates the gray background of the grid inside the plot:
> print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=diagnosis)) + geom_bar() + theme_bw()  )

Here you have changed the theme of the plot, not the plot itself.  The theme deals with thing like background color, font size, etc, but not plot elements themselves.

> # The following also produces a brightly colored plot, surprisingly:
> print(
> ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=diagnosis)) + geom_bar()
> + scale_colour_manual(values=c("gray", "black", "white"))
> )

You are attempting to change the colour aesthetic with the scale_ command, not the fill aesthetic...

> # The following makes a two-color plot and labels these colors "black" and "white" in a legend:
> print( ggplot(data=TINYDATA, aes( x=0,  y=FREQ, group=diagnosis, fill=c("black", "white", "black"))) + geom_bar() )

It thinks that "black" and "white" are levels of a categorical variable, not colors.

> There must be a simple solution?

ggplot(aes(x = 0, y = FREQ, group = diagnosis, fill = diagnosis), data = TINYDATA) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_grey()

And for colors of your choice...

ggplot(aes(x = 0, y = FREQ, group = diagnosis, fill = diagnosis), data = TINYDATA) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('A' = 'blue', 'B' = 'red', 'C' = 'green'))

Hope it helps
david.

messages.body_plain:
I don't know if **ply can pass the name of the objects given to the
function; i doubt it. In your situation I'd do a for loop, maybe with
l*ply,

library(ggplot2)

d = data.frame(id = seq(1, 100), matrix(rnorm(100 * 5), ncol = 5))

m = melt(d, id="id")

basic <- ggplot() + geom_line(aes(id, value))

plotone <- function(.col) basic %+% subset(m, variable == .col) + ylab(.col)

pdf("multiple.pdf")
l_ply(unique(m$variable), plotone, .print=T)
dev.off()

Alternatively, you could loop over the original wide format data.frame,

plotone <- function(.col) ggplot(d) +
  geom_line(aes_string(x="id", y=.col))

pdf("multiple.pdf")
l_ply(names(d)[-1], plotone, .print=T)
dev.off()

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: display regression equation with facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On scatter plots, I would like to display the regression equation in addition to the regression line obtained with stat_smooth.

I found a few examples on the web, such as:
<http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/d53807fa41b95cc0>

This involves calculating the regression line with lm() and then using geom_text() to display it on the plot.

While not particularly hard, it is a bit of a waste since the regression is calculated twice (stat_smooth and lm).

More importantly, I am working on a case where I use facet_wrap to display several groups, each in one panel, each with a regression line. I can calculate as many regressions with lm() as there are panels (thus compounding the "waste" problem just raised) but I don't know how to tell ggplot2 which equation to display in which panel.

Is there a way that I have not discovered to tell ggplot2 to display the equation for the fit produced with stat_smooth (assuming the smooth method does produce an equation)? If this option exists, ggplot2 would automatically display the appropriate equation in each panel of a facet_wrap.

Thanks in advance,

Denis

d <- data.frame(x=1, y=1, f=1:3)

  geom_point(aes(x, y), data=d) +
  geom_text(aes(x, y, label=l), data=s) +
  facet_wrap(~f)

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was trying to use ggplot2 to reproduce one of the graph I produced with lattice. It is scatter plot fit with loess smooth curve. The code for lattice is as follows:

xyplot( DV ~ IPRE, subset = (CMT==7 & MDV == 0 & DRUG==1), data = dv_ipred_pred,
xlab = "Individual fit ", ylab = "Observation ",
scales=list(x=list(relation = "same",tck=c(1,0)), y = list(relation = "same",tck=c(1,0))),
xlim=c(0,350),
ylim=c(0,350),
main = "Individual fits vs. Observation Plot (linear scale)\nRET CMT: 7",
strip=function(...) strip.default(..., strip.names=T,
strip.levels=T, style=3, sep = ": "),
layout = c(1,1),
as.table=T,
key = key.content,
panel = function(x, y, ...) {
    panel.xyplot(x,y, col="gray65", pch=1.1, cex=1.1)
    panel.abline(0,1, col="darkgray", lwd=2,lty=2)
    panel.loess(x, y, span = 1, col="black", lwd=3)
} )

The code using ggplot2 is :

ggplot(data=EPO_RET2, aes(IPRE,DV))+
geom_point(colour="grey65",size=4,shape=1)+
geom_abline(intercept=0,slope=1,linetype=2,color="darkgray",size=1.5)+

I am wondering why is that and how I can produce the similar graph as done in the lattice. Thanks

Xiaoyu

messages.subject: Re: secondary y-axis
messages.body_plain:
Hadley

Sorry to resurrect such an old thread, but I would like to ask whether it is necessary to restrict the proposed secondary y axis to only displaying a transformation of the first. I fully agree that in most situations secondary axes are confusing and best avoided. However everything has its place.

In my case I have time-series data to display in a main plot, and would like to display climatic data below it in a supportive role. I could have three graphs (data, rainfall and temperature), but this would be very cramped. It would be simpler to have one main data plot, with a subplot for rainfall (blue bars) and temperature (red line) on two axes - this is a common and very clear way of plotting climatic data.

The reader will never be comparing rainfall with temperature, rather is comparing rainfall or temperature trends with the data, so there will be little potential for misinterpretation. There is far greater potential for misinterpretation if the y axes must be shortened to accommodate a third graph, as this makes it more difficult for the reader to discern differences in the data.

I have created these plots in base graphics in the past but would like to be able to move to ggplot as it requires considerably less coding.

Every rule has an exception. Deliberate restrictions in usage to enforce what in most circumstances is correct are very frustrating for those confronted with the exception.

Thanks for an excellent package in all other respects.

Samuel

messages.body_plain:
Xiaoyu,

Regarding the gray band in the ggplot2 graph: that is the 95% confidence band on the estimate of the loess curve. It can be turned off via parameter se=FALSE to qplot(); I'm not sure of the corresponding parameter for ggplot() and related functions.

Also, Hadley's book indicates that loess is used on data sets less than 1000 points, and an alternative smoother is used on larger data sets. It looks like you might be exceeding that limit, so that you could be comparing slightly different smoothers.

- Tom

messages.subject: arranging plots, lining up axes
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering if there is a way, with some combination of ggplot2 and
gridExtra and possibly other tools, to make sets of graphs whose
horizontal axes are aligned although their labels and other decorations
may be different sizes.

  The idea here is that I have two different kinds of variables that
want to share the same x axes, but possibly have quite different
formatting otherwise.  There are basically two routes to take (I think):
one is to abuse ggplot2's model a bit and try to do this with vertical
faceting, with _post hoc_ adjustment of decorations.  The second is to
make two separate plots and arrange them on the page accordingly.

  The problem with the first approach, besides the fact that it abuses
ggplot2's underlying model, is that it's hard to make different vertical
facets very different.  In the example below it's not too bad, but it's
not hard to come up with examples where it gets much harder to hack the
formatting of the two sets.

  The problem with the second approach is that it's a great big nuisance
to tweak the plot margins to make the x axes align properly.  Presumably
to make this work properly and automatically one would need to get into
the guts of the grid object and sort out the dimensions of the actual
plot region (as opposed to the entire figure region) and make these
match ...

  Any ideas welcome.

  thanks
    Ben Bolker

=============

## make up some data with very different ranges
set.seed(1001)
z <- data.frame(x=runif(300),y=c(runif(150)*1e5,runif(150)),
                f=rep(rep(LETTERS[1:3],50),2),
                var=rep(letters[1:2],each=150))

library(ggplot2)

## choice 1: use faceting; use grid.text() to add separate axis labels

g1 <- ggplot(z,aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+facet_grid(var~f,scale="free_y")+
  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+ ## no gap
  labs(y="")

## would like to remove vertical strips: can eliminate text with
## +opts(strip.text.y=theme_blank())
## but don't know how to get rid of them entirely (without eliminating
##  background for horizontal strips?

g1
grid.text(c("first axis","second axis"),
          x=unit(rep(0.02,2), "npc"),
          y=unit(c(0.3,0.7),"npc"),
          rot = 90,
          gp=gpar(cex=1.2))

## choice 2: create two plots, then arrange using grid.arrange(),
##  with painstakingly tweaked plot.margin() to get axes in synch

zz <- split(z,z$var)
g2 <- ggplot(zz[[1]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+facet_grid(.~f)+
  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+
  labs(y="second axis")+
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_blank(),axis.title.x=theme_blank())

g3 <- ggplot(zz[[2]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+facet_grid(.~f)+
  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+
  labs(y="first axis")+
  opts(strip.text.x=theme_blank(),strip.background=theme_blank())

library(gridExtra)
## By trial and error: it seems that the margins are specified in order
## Top, Right, Bottom, Left -- different from base R standard
## which is Bottom, Left, Top, Right??
grid.arrange(g2,g3+opts(plot.margin=unit(c(0,1,0,1.25),"lines")),nrow=2)

  [Dennis: I could 'fix' the problem by making sure the y-axis labels
and title are the same width, but the whole point of this exercise is to
try to make the plots align *without* doing that ... thanks, though.]

  I've managed to get a bit farther with this, but not to solve it.  It
seems (?) that the problem occurs when one plot is constructed with a
legend and the other isn't -- even when the legend is removed with
opts(legend.position="none"), which implies that a difference in some
horizontal spacing element persists.
   The code below is somewhat simplified (doesn't depend on my
particular complicated plots) and shows that faceting is not relevant,
but presence/absence of legends is.
   Unfortunately, I don't know enough about digging into grid objects to
have been able to figure out (so far) where the difference lies and what
to do about it ...

  On a side note, I was looking at
<http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/753bd02a945a0e93>
and can offer the following little bit of code that seems to find
vertical strips (which could then be used, with a little bit work, to
adjust spacing properly in the cases shown in that e-mail) ...

    strips <- lapply(dots, function(.g) {
      cc <- .g$children$layout$children
      vstrips <- cc[grepl("^strip_v",names(cc))]
      ## assume all strips the same width/height,
      ##    so just use the first one?
      if (length(vstrips)>0)
        editGrob(vstrips[[1]],vp=NULL)
      else ggplot2:::.zeroGrob
    })

z <- data.frame(x=runif(300),y=c(runif(150)*1e5,runif(150)),

                var=rep(letters[1:2],each=150))

  labs(y=expression(log[10]("second axis")))+
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_blank(),axis.title.x=theme_blank())

  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+
  labs(y="first axis")+
  opts(strip.text.x=theme_blank(),strip.background=theme_blank())

## narrow y-axis, facets, no legend
g3 <- ggplot(zz[[2]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point(colour="red")+facet_grid(.~f)+

  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+
  labs(y="first axis")+
  opts(strip.text.x=theme_blank(),strip.background=theme_blank())

## wide y-axis, no facets, no legend
g4 <- ggplot(zz[[1]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+
  labs(y=expression(log[10]("second axis")))+
  opts(axis.text.x=theme_blank(),axis.title.x=theme_blank())

## narrow y-axis, no facets, no legend
g5 <- ggplot(zz[[2]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point(colour="red")+

  labs(y="first axis")+
  opts(strip.text.x=theme_blank(),strip.background=theme_blank())

## narrow y-axis, no facets, legend
g6 <- ggplot(zz[[2]],aes(x=x,y=y,colour=f))+geom_point()+

  labs(y="first axis")+
  opts(strip.text.x=theme_blank(),strip.background=theme_blank())

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(g1,g2,g3,g4,g5,g6,ncol=3,nrow=2) ## check all plots
library(ggExtra)
theme_set(theme_bw())

grid.newpage()
## align all plots vertically.
## numbers 2 and 6 (the ones with legends, with or without
## facets) are misaligned

grid.newpage()
## this is true even if we suppress the legends
align.plots(g1,g2+opts(legend.position="none"),g3,g4,g5,
            g6+opts(legend.position="none"))

## my (so far unsuccessful) attempts at tracking down the
## horizontal spacing differences between #5 and #6
gg5 <- ggplotGrob(g5)
gg6 <- ggplotGrob(g6+opts(legend.position="none"))

gl5 <- lapply(gg5$children$layout$children,grobWidth)
gl5[sapply(gl5,as.numeric)>0]

gg5$children$layout$children$`panel-3-3`$children[[3]]
gg6$children$layout$children$`panel-3-3`$children[[3]]

messages.subject: extreme stubbornness
messages.body_plain:
I think I solved my problem.

  The logic of legend spacing within ggplot2 turns out to be (in my
opinion) a bit odd (this is all in ggplotGrob(), in plot-render.r).

  If there is no legend generated at all (i.e. there are no aesthetics
varying within facets), but opts(position.legend) is not specified
explicitly either, then position.legend defaults to "right" and the
legend width is set to zero (the width of the legend box) plus 0.5 lines.

  If there is a legend generated and opts(position.legend) is "right" or
"left" then legend width is set to the width of the legend box plus 0.5
lines (of course).

  If opts(position.legend) is "none" then legend width **is ignored in
positioning boxes** so the width is effectively zero.

  So there is different spacing when rendering a ggplot object that has
no legend (and no legend.position set) and when rendering a ggplot
object that has a legend, but with the legend disabled via
legend.position="none".

  This means that testing for zero width of the legend in the ggplotGrob
(as the current version of align.plots() does) is not sufficient -- you
have to look at the legend position in the original ggplot object.

  I have a modified version of align.plots() that does this, and could
provide a patch, but I'm a little bit confused about where to get the
latest version of ggExtra for generating an appropriate patch: R-forge,
or googlecode?

  Arguably, the logic within ggplotGrob() could (should?) be tweaked to
*not* add 0.5 lines to legendwidth when is.zero(legend) is TRUE ...

  (As I mentioned in a previous message, I think I also have the
beginnings of a fix for the issue raised in February about taking
vertical strips into account.  Also, it would seem to be a good idea to
replace .ggplot2:::.zeroGrob with zeroGrob() [presumably this wasn't
exposed before and is now].)

  cheers
    Ben Bolker

I think the best you can do is to label the points directly:

ggplot(data, aes(tv.avg, ped.avg))+

  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) +

  geom_point(size=2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = composto), hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The ggExtra package has align.plots() implementing your second idea.
Quite an ugly hack, though, I'm afraid.

baptiste

library(ggExtra)
align.plots(g2, g3)

On Tue, May 10, 2011 at 5:14 PM, Ben Bolker <bbo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>  I'm wondering if there is a way, with some combination of ggplot2 and
> gridExtra and possibly other tools, to make sets of graphs whose
> horizontal axes are aligned although their labels and other decorations
> may be different sizes.
>
>  The idea here is that I have two different kinds of variables that
> want to share the same x axes, but possibly have quite different
> formatting otherwise.  There are basically two routes to take (I think):
> one is to abuse ggplot2's model a bit and try to do this with vertical
> faceting, with _post hoc_ adjustment of decorations.  The second is to
> make two separate plots and arrange them on the page accordingly.
>
>  The problem with the first approach, besides the fact that it abuses
> ggplot2's underlying model, is that it's hard to make different vertical
> facets very different.  In the example below it's not too bad, but it's
> not hard to come up with examples where it gets much harder to hack the
> formatting of the two sets.
>
>  The problem with the second approach is that it's a great big nuisance
> to tweak the plot margins to make the x axes align properly.  Presumably
> to make this work properly and automatically one would need to get into
> the guts of the grid object and sort out the dimensions of the actual
> plot region (as opposed to the entire figure region) and make these
> match ...
>
>  Any ideas welcome.
>
>  thanks
>    Ben Bolker
>
> =============
>
> ## make up some data with very different ranges
> set.seed(1001)
> z <- data.frame(x=runif(300),y=c(runif(150)*1e5,runif(150)),
>                f=rep(rep(LETTERS[1:3],50),2),
>                var=rep(letters[1:2],each=150))
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
> ## choice 1: use faceting; use grid.text() to add separate axis labels
>
> g1 <- ggplot(z,aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+facet_grid(var~f,scale="free_y")+
>  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+ ## no gap
>  labs(y="")
>
> ## would like to remove vertical strips: can eliminate text with
> ## +opts(strip.text.y=theme_blank())
> ## but don't know how to get rid of them entirely (without eliminating
> ##  background for horizontal strips?
>
> g1
> grid.text(c("first axis","second axis"),
>          x=unit(rep(0.02,2), "npc"),
>          y=unit(c(0.3,0.7),"npc"),
>          rot = 90,
>          gp=gpar(cex=1.2))
>
> ## choice 2: create two plots, then arrange using grid.arrange(),
> ##  with painstakingly tweaked plot.margin() to get axes in synch
>
> zz <- split(z,z$var)
> g2 <- ggplot(zz[[1]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+facet_grid(.~f)+
>  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+
>  labs(y="second axis")+
>  opts(axis.text.x=theme_blank(),axis.title.x=theme_blank())
>
> g3 <- ggplot(zz[[2]],aes(x=x,y=y))+geom_point()+facet_grid(.~f)+
>  opts(panel.margin=unit(0,"inches"))+
>  labs(y="first axis")+
>  opts(strip.text.x=theme_blank(),strip.background=theme_blank())
>
> library(gridExtra)
> ## By trial and error: it seems that the margins are specified in order
> ## Top, Right, Bottom, Left -- different from base R standard
> ## which is Bottom, Left, Top, Right??
> grid.arrange(g2,g3+opts(plot.margin=unit(c(0,1,0,1.25),"lines")),nrow=2)
>

messages.subject: Remove whitespace between margins when using grid graphics
messages.subject_clean: Remove whitespace between margins when using grid graphics
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have seen some tips on how to adjust margins of ggplot graphics
(plot.margin in opts), but is there a way to simply remove whitespace
between plots?

Consider the following example:

require(ggplot2)

a <- qplot(a, b, data = data.frame(a=rnorm(20), b=rnorm(20)), geom =
"point") +
  opts(axis.text.x = theme_blank()) +
  labs(x="")
b <- qplot(a, b, data = data.frame(a=rnorm(20), b=rnorm(20)), geom =
"point")

pdf("plot.pdf")
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2,2)))
vplayout <- function(x, y)
  viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)
print(a, vp = vplayout(1, 1))
print(b, vp = vplayout(2, 1))
print(a, vp = vplayout(1, 2))
print(b, vp = vplayout(2, 2))
dev.off()

I want to easily remove most of the whitespace between the upper two
plots and the lower two plots (or between left and right hand plots)
without having to adjust margins of all the plots using plot.margin).

Thanks! Scott

messages.subject_clean: Remove whitespace between margins when using grid graphics
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one way, playing around with the positions of viewports in
grid. I also stripped out the plot.background().

a <- qplot(a, b, data = data.frame(a=rnorm(20), b=rnorm(20)),
           geom = "point") +

     opts(axis.text.x = theme_blank(), plot.background = theme_blank()) +

     labs(x="")
b <- qplot(a, b, data = data.frame(a=rnorm(20), b=rnorm(20)),

           geom = "point") + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())

vp1 <- viewport(width = 0.54, height = 0.54, x = 0.27, y = 0.27)
vp2 <- viewport(width = 0.54, height = 0.54, x = 0.27, y = 0.75)
vp3 <- viewport(width = 0.54, height = 0.54, x = 0.76, y = 0.26)
vp4 <- viewport(width = 0.54, height = 0.54, x = 0.76, y = 0.75)

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2,2)))
print(b, vp = vp1)
print(a, vp = vp2)
print(b, vp = vp3)
print(a, vp = vp4)

You can play around with the widths and heights to control the size of
a viewport; x and y define the center position of the viewport.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: extreme stubbornness
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, May 10, 2011 at 10:33 PM, Ben Bolker <bbo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>  I think I solved my problem.

Glad to hear this.

>
>  The logic of legend spacing within ggplot2 turns out to be (in my
> opinion) a bit odd (this is all in ggplotGrob(), in plot-render.r).

I second that opinion.

>
>  If there is no legend generated at all (i.e. there are no aesthetics
> varying within facets), but opts(position.legend) is not specified
> explicitly either, then position.legend defaults to "right" and the
> legend width is set to zero (the width of the legend box) plus 0.5 lines.
>
>  If there is a legend generated and opts(position.legend) is "right" or
> "left" then legend width is set to the width of the legend box plus 0.5
> lines (of course).
>
>  If opts(position.legend) is "none" then legend width **is ignored in
> positioning boxes** so the width is effectively zero.
>
>  So there is different spacing when rendering a ggplot object that has
> no legend (and no legend.position set) and when rendering a ggplot
> object that has a legend, but with the legend disabled via
> legend.position="none".
>
>  This means that testing for zero width of the legend in the ggplotGrob
> (as the current version of align.plots() does) is not sufficient -- you
> have to look at the legend position in the original ggplot object.
>
>  I have a modified version of align.plots() that does this, and could
> provide a patch, but I'm a little bit confused about where to get the
> latest version of ggExtra for generating an appropriate patch: R-forge,
> or googlecode?

googlecode, which is later automatically passed to r-forge. You may
also send me directly your modified file.

>  Arguably, the logic within ggplotGrob() could (should?) be tweaked to
> *not* add 0.5 lines to legendwidth when is.zero(legend) is TRUE ...
>
>  (As I mentioned in a previous message, I think I also have the
> beginnings of a fix for the issue raised in February about taking
> vertical strips into account.
> Also, it would seem to be a good idea to
> replace .ggplot2:::.zeroGrob with zeroGrob() [presumably this wasn't
> exposed before and is now].)

I think that's correct. It's kind of sad that we have 3 grobs of this
type in 3 packages: grid::nullGrob, ggplot2::zeroGrob,
gridExtra::virtualGrob. I wonder if zeroGrob could be moved to grid
(then gridExtra could use it without requiring a heavy dependency).

Cheers,

baptiste

>
>  cheers
>    Ben Bolker
>

messages.subject: Re: problem with variables within ggplot() function
messages.subject_clean: problem with variables within ggplot() function
messages.body_plain:
Hi jyk -

It's very hard to tell what you want to do.  Generally speaking you should always make use of the scoping rules used by ggplot2 - never refer to variable names in the way that you do (e.g. colnames(A)[i]).  Refer to them directly as X1, X2, or X3.  If you need to do it for a bunch of them, melt the data.frame.  Maybe these examples provide a basis to launch from?

library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(30),
  y = rnorm(30),
  z = rnorm(30),
  a = sample(paste('a', 1:3, sep = ''), 10, replace = TRUE),
  b = sample(paste('b', 1:3, sep = ''), 10, replace = TRUE),
  c = sample(paste('c', 1:3, sep = ''), 10, replace = TRUE)
)
mdf <- melt(df, id.vars = c('a','b','c'))

qplot(value, data = mdf, geom = 'density', colour = variable, facets = a ~ .)

mdf <- melt(mdf, id.vars = c('variable','value')) # better way to do this from df?
names(mdf) <- c('contvar', 'value', 'catvar', 'cohort')

qplot(value, data = mdf, geom = 'density', colour = cohort,
  facets = catvar ~ contvar)

Hope it helps
david.

Another option would be to use aes_string() instead of aes() to define your variables, then it should work. Here is an example (without data).

colstart=3

colend=6

for (i in colstart:colend){

plot<-ggplot()+

geom_boxplot(data=df.data, aes_string(x= paste(colnames(df.data)[2]), y= paste(colnames(df.data)[i])))+

theme_bw()

#save plot

ggsave(sprintf("Boxplot.%s.png", colnames(df.data)[i]), width=6, height=6)

}

HTH,

Brandon

messages.subject: Re: legend control
messages.body_plain:
Hi

> 1 – how to control the legend position? For some reasons I do not
> understand the “legend.position” statement under “opts” seems now not
> working at all

This is because you set theme *after* setting opts. So, set theme
before setting opts.
And there is no option named "legend.title."

> 2 – how to set the legend so that the order of each item is the same
> as given in the vector “data$composto”? The legend items seem to be
> formatted in an alphabetical order by default, how to override this?

If X is factor, the order of the levels of X determines the order of
the legend. This is only way to control the order.
So re-level the variable before using ggplot like this:

data$composto <- factor(data$composto, levels=as.character(data$composto))

> 3 – is it possible to split the legend for each corresponding facet on
> the plot? I have no clue for this…

probably no.

--

messages.subject: Re: legend control
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

sorry, actually there is an option named "legend.title", but it does
not one controlling the text of legend title, but controlling the
*style* of legend title.

title label of the legend is determined by
1) name of the scale, by passing e.g., scale_colour_hue("composto",
h=c(0, 360)). so actually you did it.
2) label setting by + labs(x="hoge", colour="composto", etc, etc)
3) specification in aes. so ggplot(aes(colour=hoge)) and (1) and (2)
are undefined, then "hoge" is the legend title of colour.

> how to control the order of facets ? (by default they seem in an
> alfabetical order)

It is same as control the order of legend. Re-level the variable for facet.

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

messages.body_snippet:
Hi,

sorry, actually there is an option named "legend.title", but it does
not one controlling the text of legend title, but controlling the
*style* of legend title.

title label of the legend is deter

messages.subject: Re: legend control
messages.body_plain:
yes, perfect!

and the very very last question: in case I want to label just some
points (not all) what is the best solution to accomplish that?
in my case just imagine I want to label the point corrisponding to
following "composto": PCB-77 and PCB-114 and 2,3,7,8-TCD and 2,3,7,8-
TCF and not the rest of points...

I can label all points but not just some of them

max

> sorry, actually there is an option named "legend.title", but it does

> *style* of legend title.
>
> title label of the legend is determined by
> 1) name of the scale, by passing e.g., scale_colour_hue("composto",
> h=c(0, 360)). so actually you did it.
> 2) label setting by + labs(x="hoge", colour="composto", etc, etc)
> 3) specification in aes. so ggplot(aes(colour=hoge)) and (1) and (2)
> are undefined, then "hoge" is the legend title of colour.
>
> > how to control the order of facets ? (by default they seem in an
> > alfabetical order)
>
> It is same as control the order of legend. Re-level the variable for facet.

messages.body_plain:
Hi

Probably it is easiest way to subset the data for geom_text:

+ geom_text(aes(label=composto, x = tv.avg, y = ped.avg),
data=subset(data,
composto%in%c("PCB-77","PCB-114","2,3,7,8-TCDD","2,3,7,8-\nTCDF")),

colour="black", size=2.5, hjust=0, vjust=0)

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

messages.subject: How to make sure xlim and ylim are the same without explicitly specifying them?
messages.subject_clean: How to make sure xlim and ylim are the same without explicitly specifying them?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I want to say a set of points after rotation are still similar to the
original ones. Therefore, I want the xlim and ylim be the same. But I
don't want to specify xlim and ylim explicity. I'm wondering if there
is an option so that qplot can figure out itself.

I also want the scaling be the same for both x and y axis. Currently,
I have to control the dimension of the output file. But I'd rather to
have something in the related to qplot function. Is there some option
that can control the x and y scaling?

set.seed(0)
m=10
X=data.frame(V1=rnorm(m), V2=rnorm(m))

prcomp_result=prcomp(X)

Y=do.call(
    rbind
    , lapply(
        1:nrow(X)
        , function(i) {
          x=X[i,]
          #browser()
          data.frame(
              V1=sum((x-prcomp_result$center)*prcomp_result$rotation[,1])
              , V2=sum((x-prcomp_result$center)*prcomp_result$rotation[,2])
              )
        }
        )
    )

tmp=rbind(
    data.frame(X, type='X')
    , data.frame(Y, type='Y')
    )

library(ggplot2)
p=qplot(V1, V2, data=tmp)+facet_grid(.~type)+xlim(-2,2)+ylim(-2,2)
ggsave(p, file=outfile, width=14, height=7)

--
Regards,
Peng

messages.subject: Re: density strips in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I played around with this a bit and came up with the following for the
given example:

df2 <- data.frame(a   = rep(c("a","b","c"), each = 200),
                  b   =   c(rnorm(200, 1.25, .35),
                             rnorm(200, -.5, .15),
                             rnorm(200,  2, 1)))

ggplot(df2, aes(x = b, y = a)) +

    stat_density(aes(fill =  ..density..), geom = "tile") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "gray75", high = "gray0",

                               limits = c(.05,3)) +
    facet_grid(a ~ ., scales = 'free_y', space = 'free') +
    opts(axis.text.y = theme_blank())

I like the concept of this graphic; I could see potential for it to
replace rug plots and even boxplots, particularly when the sample
sizes are large and the variable is continuous (at least in
principle). Someone should give serious consideration to creating a
geom for it :)

Cheers,
Dennis

messages.subject: R development master class: SF, June 8-9
messages.subject_clean: R development master class: SF, June 8-9
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I hope you don't mind the slightly off topic email, but I'm going to
be teaching an R development master class in San Francisco on June
8-9.  The basic idea of the class is to help you write better code,
focused on the mantra of "do not repeat yourself". In day one you will
learn powerful new tools of abstraction, allowing you to solve a wider
range of problems with fewer lines of code. Day two will teach you how
to make packages, the fundamental unit of code distribution in R,
allowing others to save time by allowing them to use your code.

To get the most out of this course, you should have some experience
programming in R already: you should be familiar with writing
functions, and the basic data structures of R: vectors, matrices,
arrays, lists and data frames. You will find the course particularly
useful if you're an experienced R user looking to take the next step,
or if you're moving to R from other programming languages and you want
to quickly get up to speed with R's unique features.

Both days will incorporate a mix of lectures and hands-on learning.
Expect to learn about a topic and then immediately put it into
practice with a small example. Plenty of help will be available if you
get stuck - there will be one assistant for every 10 attendees. You'll
receive a printed copy of all slides, as well as electronic access to
the slides, code and data. The material covered in the course is
currently being turned into a book. You can access the current draft
at https://github.com/hadley/devtools/wiki/.

More information, including a complete session outline for the two
days is available at:
http://www.revolutionanalytics.com/products/training/public/r-development.php

Regards,

Hadley

PS.  I'm also offering an internet version of the day one through
statistics.com <http://statistics.com> -
http://www.statistics.com/courses/using-r/r-program-adv/

--

Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

I wanted to enlarge all text-setting by modifying the base_size of the
theme but I realized that it does not seem to work if I use facets:

ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()

# large text, no facets
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 18))
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()

# small text, facets
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 8))
ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap( ~ z)

opts(axis.text.x <- theme_text(size = 18, colour = "red", angle = 90))

What is wrong with my code???

Antje

tm <- theme_bw(base_size=12)

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Try this:

library(ggplot2)
all <- data.frame(Source = rep(c('group1', 'group2'), each = 100),
                  value = rnorm(200, m = rep(c(0, 3), each = 100)))
medians <- ddply(all, .(Source), summarise, med.x = signif(median(value), 3),
                   med.y = signif(median(density(value)$y), 3))

g <- ggplot(all, aes(x=value)) +
        geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..), fill="lightsteelblue") +

        geom_density(adjust=1.5, size=1, linetype="longdash") +

        facet_grid(Source ~ .) +  labs(x = "x", y = "density") +
        geom_text(data = medians, aes(x= med.x, y=med.y, label=med.x))
print(g)

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
I believe this is a bug in ggplot. The bars extend to the other categories when they are NA. Here's a workaround filling the NA with 0.

library(ggplot2)
dat <-read.csv("http://dl.dropbox.com/u/389960/x.csv", head=T)
attach(dat)
ggplot(dat,aes(xyz,Plan,na.rm=T,FUN=sum),Plan,fill=State) +
facet_wrap(~State,nrow=1) + geom_bar(stat="identity", width = 0.2 ) + coord_flip()

dat2 <- reshape(dat, idvar = "xyz", timevar = "State", direction = "wide")

dat2[is.na <http://is.na>(dat2)] <- 0

dat3 <- reshape(dat2, idvar = "xyz", varying = grep("Plan", names(dat2)),
                direction = "long")
names(dat3)[2] <- "State"
ggplot(dat3,aes(xyz,Plan,na.rm=T,FUN=sum),Plan,fill=State) +
facet_wrap(~State,nrow=1) + geom_bar(stat="identity", width = 0.2 )+
coord_flip()

HTH

Luciano

messages.body_plain:

Hash: SHA1

On 11-05-16 09:58 AM, Hadley Wickham wrote:
>> Every rule has an exception. Deliberate restrictions in usage to enforce
>> what in most circumstances is correct are very frustrating for those
>> confronted with the exception.
>
> I understand your point, and your frustration, but it's extremely
> unlikely that this sort of dual-scale plot will ever be possible in
> ggplot2. I have so little development time to spend on ggplot2 that I
> can only spend on those problems that I think are most important, and
> while I might be persuaded to not hate double-axis plots, you'll never
> be able to persuade me enough to love them enough to implement them.
>
> Hadley
>

  To chime in here: I think the point that may not be appreciated is
that the restriction that secondary y-axes are only allowed as
transformations of a primary axis is not (I think) a *deliberate*
restriction, but one that stems from the (sophisticated/complicated)
architecture of ggplot2.

  I would also be tempted to nominate Hadley's reply as a fortune()
candidate: in the generic format,

I understand your point, and your frustration, but it's extremely

unlikely that [FEATURE X] will ever be possible in [PACKAGE Y]. I have
so little development time to spend on [PACKAGE Y] that I can only spend

on those problems that I think are most important, and while I might be

persuaded to not hate [FEATURE X], you'll never be able to persuade me
enough to love them enough to implement [them/it].

  (substitute your favorite combination of feature and package here ...)

  Also note that we are talking here about a hypothetical extension
(arbitrary secondary y-axes) to a hypothetical extension (y-axes based
on transformations of a primary y-axis) that doesn't exist yet (and may
itself be pretty far down on Hadley's to-do list) ... if I were you and
wanted arbitrary secondary y-axes, I would start hacking around with the
grid.xaxis and grid.yaxis functions in the grid package and see if I
could adjust the layout of an existing ggplot (converted a grid object
via ggplotGrob() -- see the align.plots function in the ggExtra package
for examples of plot-hacking)

  Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Support for jags and (open)bugs?
messages.body_plain:
I'm beginning to do more Bayesian analysis using jags and occasionally OpenBUGS.  There are various packages that help one set up, run, and then analyze those results inside of R; I've tried rjags and am currently using R2jags.  As you can see in the example in the R2jags manual (http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/R2jags/index.html) for the jags command, they use plot, traceplot, xyplot, and densityplot to analyze results that are of class rjags or mcmc.list.  They seem to use base graphics and lattice.

Has anyone produced similar functions that use ggplot2 for working with these data types or other types produced by jags or perhaps openbugs?  I haven't found anything searching in this mailing list.

Thanks,

Bill

messages.subject: Re: Support for jags and (open)bugs?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Bill,

Using as an example the school dataset from R2WinBUGS package (see its vignette):

library(rjags)
library(coda)
library(ggplot2)
library(R2WinBUGS)

data(schools)
schoolmodel <- function(){
  for (j in 1:J)
    {
      y[j] ~ dnorm (theta[j], tau.y[j])
      theta[j] ~ dnorm (mu.theta, tau.theta)
      tau.y[j] <- pow(sigma.y[j], -2)
    }
  mu.theta ~ dnorm (0.0, 1.0E-6)
  tau.theta <- pow(sigma.theta, -2)
  sigma.theta ~ dunif (0, 1000)
}
write.model(schoolmodel, "~/schoolmodel.bug")
J <- nrow(schools)
y <- schools$estimate
sigma.y <- schools$sd
forJags <- list(J = nrow(schools), y = schools$estimate, sigma.y = schools$sd)
inits <- function(){
  list(theta = rnorm(J, 0, 100), mu.theta = rnorm(1, 0, 100),
       sigma.theta = runif(1, 0, 100))
}

school.sim <- jags.model(file = "schoolmodel.bug", data = forJags,
                         inits = inits, n.chains = 3)
school.out <- coda.samples(school.sim, variable.names =
                           c("theta", "mu.theta", "sigma.theta"),
                           n.iter = 1000)
summary(school.out)

Than you can either use the mcmcplots packages which gives a "feel" of ggplot2:

library(mcmcplots)
denplot(school.out, parms = c('mu.theta', collapse = FALSE, auto.layout = TRUE))

Or go with ggplot2 after extracting the info you want from your output, like for example:

mu.theta.out <- cbind(school.out[[1]][,1], school.out[[2]][,1], school.out[[3]][,1])
attributes(mu.theta.out) <- NULL
dens.mu.theta <- density(mu.theta.out)
q25.mu.theta <- quantile(mu.theta.out, .025)
q975.mu.theta <- quantile(mu.theta.out, .975)
dd.mu.theta <- with(dens.mu.theta, data.frame(x,y))

To get a density plot for mu.theta with its 95% credible interval:

qplot(x, y, data = dd.mu.theta, geom = "line", ylab = "", xlab = "") +
  geom_ribbon(data = subset(dd.mu.theta, x>q25.mu.theta & x<q975.mu.theta),
              aes(ymax = y), ymin = 0, fill = "red", colour = NA, alpha = 0.5)

Denis

messages.subject: Re: special characters in column names
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, May 9, 2011 at 1:51 AM, july <antje.ni...@googlemail.com> wrote:
> I've tested it once more. It does not work with aes_string. Is there
> anything wrong?:
>
> library(ggplot2)
>
> df <- data.frame(c(1:10),c(10:1))
>
> # works with simple column names
> names(df) <- c("name1","name2")
> parameter <- "name1"
> ggplot(df, aes_string(x = parameter, y = parameter)) + geom_point()
>
> # does not work with special characters in column names
> names(df) <- c("Special name(1)","Special name(2)")
> parameter <- "Special name(1)"
> ggplot(df, aes_string(x = parameter, y = parameter)) + geom_point()

You want:

names(df) <- c("Special name(1)","Special name(2)")
parameter <- "`Special name(1)`"
ggplot(df, aes_string(x = parameter, y = parameter)) + geom_point()

When you have non-syntactic names, you need to surround them in `.

Hadley

messages.subject: Getting a stacked barchard
messages.body_plain:
I have a barchart that looks good to me but I have a request to change
it from a side-by-side chart (which makes the most sense to me) to
stacked

Data consists of sales figures by month for different products for two
divisions of a company

The idea would be to produce stacked bars for the number of products
sold by division by month..

At the moment I'm stumped.  Am I missing something obvious or do I
need to reshape my data or what?

Any help would be appreciated.

Simple example of what I've done so far.
===============================

library(ggplot2, reshape2)
df1 <- structure(list(prod = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L,
3L), .Label = c("x",
"y", "z"), class = "factor"), jan = c(10L, 15L, 20L, 20L, 15L,
10L), feb = c(10L, 18L, 10L, 15L, 18L, 10L), march = c(10L, 10L,
34L, 17L, 34L, 18L), group = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L,
2L), .Label = c("a", "b"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("prod",
"jan", "feb", "march", "group"), class = "data.frame", row.names =
c(NA,
-6L))

df2 <- melt(df1,id= c("prod","group"))
str(df2)

p <- ggplot(df2, aes(prod, value, fill=group))
p <- p + facet_grid(.~ variable)
p <- p + geom_bar(stat = "identity", position="dodge") +
     xlab("Products") + ylab("Sales")  +
     opts(title = "Monthly Sales Breakdown") +
      scale_fill_discrete('Group')
p

==================================

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, May 15, 2011 at 1:14 AM, Ben Bolker <bbo...@gmail.com> wrote:
> -----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----
> Hash: SHA1
>
> On 11-05-16 09:58 AM, Hadley Wickham wrote:
>>> Every rule has an exception. Deliberate restrictions in usage to enforce
>>> what in most circumstances is correct are very frustrating for those
>>> confronted with the exception.
>>
>> I understand your point, and your frustration, but it's extremely
>> unlikely that this sort of dual-scale plot will ever be possible in
>> ggplot2. I have so little development time to spend on ggplot2 that I
>> can only spend on those problems that I think are most important, and
>> while I might be persuaded to not hate double-axis plots, you'll never
>> be able to persuade me enough to love them enough to implement them.
>>
>> Hadley
>>
>
>  To chime in here: I think the point that may not be appreciated is
> that the restriction that secondary y-axes are only allowed as
> transformations of a primary axis is not (I think) a *deliberate*
> restriction, but one that stems from the (sophisticated/complicated)
> architecture of ggplot2.
>
>  I would also be tempted to nominate Hadley's reply as a fortune()
> candidate: in the generic format,
>
> I understand your point, and your frustration, but it's extremely
> unlikely that [FEATURE X] will ever be possible in [PACKAGE Y]. I have
> so little development time to spend on [PACKAGE Y] that I can only spend
> on those problems that I think are most important, and while I might be
> persuaded to not hate [FEATURE X], you'll never be able to persuade me
> enough to love them enough to implement [them/it].
>
>  (substitute your favorite combination of feature and package here ...)
>
>  Also note that we are talking here about a hypothetical extension
> (arbitrary secondary y-axes) to a hypothetical extension (y-axes based
> on transformations of a primary y-axis) that doesn't exist yet (and may
> itself be pretty far down on Hadley's to-do list) ... if I were you and
> wanted arbitrary secondary y-axes, I would start hacking around with the
> grid.xaxis and grid.yaxis functions in the grid package and see if I
> could adjust the layout of an existing ggplot (converted a grid object
> via ggplotGrob() -- see the align.plots function in the ggExtra package
> for examples of plot-hacking)
>

A major issue here is that ggplot2 does not use Grid axes but defines
its own (as I recall, not working with native units); it makes such
custom changes more difficult, if at all possible. My version of the
above request would be to facilitate the work of people willing to
extend ggplot2 with grid functions (as lattice does); I believe it is
already going this way in the current package overhaul.

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: secondary y-axis
messages.body_plain:
I don't expect someone else to develop a new feature for me. I was just under the impression from the earlier posts that Hadley was already intending to implement a secondary axis but only as a transformation of the first axis.

"And it will never be possible to add a secondary scale, just an secondary axes that is a transformation of the primary." (Hadley)

This may no longer be on the priority list though, which I understand.

My point is that as soon as a secondary axis is available, even if trained on the same data, the first thing some users will start doing is producing scaled datasets where one variable matches the secondary axis, as a dirty workaround, and you'll immediately have dual-axis plots available in ggplot2. Any feature will be pushed to its limits, that's what people do.

Knowing how users will mistreat it anyway, it might be useful to code the second axis more generically from the start to allow people to extend it in this way more flexibly. Or follow baptiste's suggestion to provide a even more generic method of modifying this.

But if the transformed secondary axis has dropped off the plans entirely my suggestion may be irrelevant. Or maybe it's just unpalatable (good point Adam)!

Thanks,
Samuel

messages.subject: Re: Getting a stacked barchard
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I was playing around with the idea of using line graphs instead of
stacked bar charts in John Kane's data and ran across a couple of
things that are useful to note (although the graphs aren't that pretty
;)

(1) It's a bad idea to conflate variable names with names of ggplot2
aesthetics; once again, group is a culprit:

> str(df2)
'data.frame':   18 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ prod    : Factor w/ 3 levels "x","y","z": 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 ...
 $ group   : Factor w/ 2 levels "a","b": 1 1 1 2 2 2 1 1 1 2 ...
 $ variable: Factor w/ 3 levels "jan","feb","march": 1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 ...
 $ value   : int  10 15 20 20 15 10 10 18 10 15 ...

> ggplot(df2, aes(x = variable, y = value, color = prod)) +
+       geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line(aes(group = prod), size = 1) +
+       facet_wrap( ~ group, ncol = 1)
Error in names(out) <- names(x) :
  'names' attribute [5] must be the same length as the vector [0]

Now change the data by replacing group with gp:

> str(df2)
'data.frame':   18 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ prod    : Factor w/ 3 levels "x","y","z": 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2 3 1 ...
 $ gp      : Factor w/ 2 levels "a","b": 1 1 1 2 2 2 1 1 1 2 ...
 $ variable: Factor w/ 3 levels "jan","feb","march": 1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 ...
 $ value   : int  10 15 20 20 15 10 10 18 10 15 ...

# Same code except for name of variable (group -> gp) now works:
> p3 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x = variable, y = value, color = prod)) +
+       geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line(aes(group = prod), size = 1) +
+       labs(x = 'Month', y = 'Sales', color = 'Product') +
+       facet_wrap(~ gp, ncol = 1)
> p3
# No error, plot renders (OK, I added a line :)

Message: when using ggplot2, don't use variable names that correspond
to ggplot2 aesthetics, such as group, colo(u)r, fill, shape, etc.,
because it may come back to bite you :) The problem arose because I
used a group aesthetic in the plot call when the data contained a
variable named group. A clash results.

(2) In the labs() statement, color = 'Product' doesn't work, but
colour = 'Product' does (after changing color to colour in the
ggplot() statement as well). Another color/colour infelicity to add to
the list...

FWIW,
Dennis

messages.subject: scale colour question
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Simple question (aren't they always?)

Hadley kindly helped me to set this up a long time ago, during a break
from a lecture, but having trouble with simple parameter switches now.

What's going on here? Take a table like that formed by the simple
code:

t <- c(6,12,18,6,12,18)
tend <- c(12,18,19,12,18,19)
act <- c("?","on","?","off","on","off")
d <- c(1,1,1,2,2,2)
inc <- data.frame(d,t,act,tend)

Run this code:

qplot(xmin=t, xmax=tend, ymin=d-0.45, ymax=d+0.45, data=inc,
geom="rect", fill=act) + scale_y_reverse("Day", breaks = 1:2) +
scale_x_continuous("Time") + scale_fill_grey(name = "Activity", breaks
= c("?","off","on"), labels = c("Not recorded", "Off nest", "On
Nest"))

And get a nice looking figure.

However, if I wanted to do something like change the colors on the
bars, I'd figure something like this should work:

qplot(xmin=t, xmax=tend, ymin=d-0.45, ymax=d+0.45, data=inc,
geom="rect", fill=act) + scale_y_reverse("Day", breaks = 1:2) +
scale_x_continuous("Time") + scale_colour_manual(name = "Activity",
values=c("red","blue","green"), breaks = c("?","off","on"), labels =
c("Not recorded", "Off nest", "On Nest"))

But no dice--it's just giving me default colors of some sort. A clue
seems to be that in the first plot, the legend is correctly labeled
(with the name and labels argument from the scale parameter), but in
the second plot, the legend is formed by the column header and levels
in that column...

Any help would be appreciated. Thanks!

Eliot

messages.subject: Re: how to add different text in different panels using ggplot?
messages.subject_clean: how to add different text in different panels using ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
It's not all that pretty, but you could add a new layer with vertical
lines at your medians.

g <- ggplot(all, aes(x=value)) +
        geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..), fill="lightsteelblue") +
        geom_density(adjust=1.5, size=1, linetype="longdash") +
        facet_grid(Source ~ .) +  labs(x = "x", y = "density") +
        geom_text(data = medians, aes(x= med.x, y=med.y, label=med.x))

+
        geom_vline(aes(xintercept = med.x), data = medians)
print(g)

messages.subject: single plot within for loop
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have lots of different datasets that I want to "ovelay" onto a
single plot within a single file. The desired output can be seen
here:
http://people.brandeis.edu/~dcaffrey/tmp/desired.pdf

The problem is that I need to iterate over each dataset using a for
loop and the for loop insists on writing each plot to a separate page
when writing to pdfas shown here:
http://people.brandeis.edu/~dcaffrey/tmp/test.pdf
When writing to jpg or X11 the last plot overwrites all previous plots
generated within the loop.

Most of the code is pasted below, and I'd appreciate any suggestions.

Thanks,
Daniel

p <- ggplot(data) + scale_x_continuous('Non-synonymous polymorphisms /
CD length',limits=c(0,0.01))

p <- p + scale_y_continuous( 'Density',limits=c(0,300))

p <- p + opts(panel.background = theme_rect(size=0))

p <- p + opts(panel.grid.minor = theme_blank())

p <- p + opts (axis.text.x =
theme_text(hjust=1,size=7,colour="black"))

p <- p +
opts(axis.title.x=theme_text(size=10,colour="black",vjust=0))

p <- p +  annotate("text",x=x,y=y,label="Gene sets:",vjust = -2, hjust
= 0,size = 4)

allRowsOfInterest <- c()

lastIndex <- length(gosOfInterest)
for (i in 1: length(gosOfInterest)){
    columnName <-
paste("hasGoTermThatIsDescendentOf",gosOfInterest[i],sep="")
    column <-  which(names(data) == columnName)
    data[,column] <- gsub("TRUE",preferredName[i],data[,column])
    data[,column] <- gsub("FALSE","Other",data[,column])
    rowsOfInterest <- which(data[,column] == preferredName[i])
    allRowsOfInterest <- c(allRowsOfInterest , rowsOfInterest)
    curData <- data[rowsOfInterest,]
    y <- y-dec
     #ITERATION 1 is written to page 1 of PDF
     if (i==1){
       pdf(file="test.pdf",onefile=TRUE)
       one <- curData
       p <- p  + geom_density(aes(x=one
$nsNormBySize),linetype=2,colour=set[i]) +
annotate("text",x=x,y=y,label=preferredName[i],vjust = -2, hjust =
0,size = 4,colour=set[i])
       print(p)
     }
     #For simplicity, lastIndex is 2 and these plots are written to
the 2nd page. I want them to be overlaid on top of the plots in the
1st page
     if (i==lastIndex){
       two <- curData
       p <- p  + geom_density(aes(x=two
$nsNormBySize),linetype=2,colour=set[i]) +
annotate("text",x=x,y=y,label=preferredName[i],vjust = -2, hjust =
0,size = 4,colour=set[i])
       i <- i+1
       rowsOfInterest  <- unique(allRowsOfInterest)
       #combined genes
       combinedData <- data[rowsOfInterest,]
       y <- y-dec
       p <- p  + geom_density(aes(x=combinedData
$nsNormBySize),colour=set[i]) + annotate("text",x=x,y=y,label="All
Gene sets",vjust = -2, hjust = 0,size = 4,colour=set[i])
       #other genes
       numOfRows <- dim(data)[1]
       allRowNums <- seq(from=1,to=numOfRows,by=1)
       matched  <- allRowNums%in%allRowsOfInterest
       allOtherData <- data[!matched,]
       y <- y-dec
       p <- p + geom_density(aes(x=allOtherData
$nsNormBySize),colour="black") +   annotate("text",x=x,y=y,label="Rest
of genome",vjust = -2, hjust = 0,size = 4)
       print(p)
     }

}
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: Symbol Size in Legend Key
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I don't think you'll be able to trick it with the opts() statement you
used, but this worked for me (pure ad hockery :)

qplot(date, value, color=variable, data=x.m, size=I(1/2)) +
   geom_smooth(aes(color = variable), alpha = 0, size = 1, se = FALSE)

alpha represents alpha transparency - lower values make it more
transparent. alpha = 0 makes the line/curve disappear :) Using size =
1 thickens the line enough to overwrite the small dot in the legend.
By default, geom_smooth() will plot standard error envelopes around
the curve; se = FALSE suppresses them.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: 2d error representation on scatterplot
messages.body_plain:
I am comparing two continuous variables in a scatterplot, to see how the relationship between them changes as a result of two different factors. In my real dataset I want to illustrate how the mean of value1 increases with factor1, while the mean of value2 decreases with factor1, while displaying the relationship with factor2 at the same time. For this I need to display error in some way.

The data can be displayed as a faceted scatterplot:

w <- data.frame("value1" = c(2:5)+rnorm(480), "value2" = c(5:2)+rnorm(480), "factor1" = as.factor(rep(1:4,120)), "factor2" = as.factor(rep(rep(1:3,each=4),40)))
p <- ggplot(w, aes(value1, value2))
f <- facet_grid(factor1 ~ factor2)
p + f + geom_point()

I am not sure how best to illustrate the means and error values on this though. I can display the range of either value individually with a boxplot:
p + f + geom_boxplot() + geom_point(colour = "red")

However I need to display both, and would prefer to just present means and sem. Two crossed error bars would do the job (a rangefinder plot), or I could use something more specific like a bagplot. However I can't figure out how to create these in ggplot2. And I may well be going about this the wrong way anyway, there could be a much simpler way of displaying this data I haven't thought of.

Any suggestions would be appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: Symbol Size in Legend Key
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Drat. I can see the smooths now - the eyes aren't what they used to
be, sorry. There is an alpha = argument in geom_smooth(), but as you
noted, it doesn't have an effect on the transparency of the smooths -
alpha = 0 looked the same as alpha = 1. In retrospect, if it had
worked, the transparency would have transferred to the legend as well;
that issue has come up before in this group.

Unfortunately, without such a trick it will be hard to resize the
points in the legend, because you set the point size in the qplot()
call and that gets transferred from the plot to the legend. None of
the opts() involving legend, AFAIK, allows modification of the
aesthetic itself (in this case, the points) and scale_colour_manual()
doesn't have an option for modifying the size of the point. I hope I'm
wrong about that and corrected, because such a feature would be useful
to know.

I tried to create a factor sz with three levels for a size aesthetic
but with a constant value 0.5 for each observation, but couldn't get
rid of the second legend even though I tried about five different ways
I know that have worked in other contexts. One in particular that I
thought should have worked but didn't was

qplot(date, value, color=variable, data=x.m2, size = sz) +
scale_size(legend = FALSE)

I'm out of ideas for trying to trick ggplot2 in that sense.

If no correction is forthcoming and you can live with the smooths in
the plot, then you can get the thicker lines in the legend. Without
them, you may be out of luck - but as I said, I hope I'm wrong in that
opinion. I'm aware that there is some development work going on to
'decouple' the legends from the plot, but it is not implemented yet in
the released version of ggplot2.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: single plot within for loop
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luciano,
Thank you for your feedback. I've provided a simpler example (still
uses data.frames as this will help me put things in context).
Basically, I want to generate densities for different subsets (rows)
of the data.frame based on whether a particular parameter is true or
false. All densities should be displayed on a single plot whereas the
example below writes them to separate pages. As my real dataset has
lots of these parameters, I decided to write a for loop. I've spent
several days on this, so I really appreciate any suggestions.
Thanks,
Daniel

library(ggplot2)

#next 7 lines create a sample dataset
myParams <- c("param1","param2","param3")
myColors <- c("red","green","blue")
values <- runif(500,min=0,max=2)
param1 <- c(rep(TRUE,300),rep(FALSE,200))
param2 <- c(rep(TRUE,200),rep(FALSE,300))
param3 <- c(rep(TRUE,50),rep(FALSE,450))
myDf <- data.frame(values,param1,param2,param3)

#Here I loop over my parameters and attempt to plot densities for each
one.
p <- ggplot(myDf)
pdf(file="simpleTest.pdf")
for ( i in 1:length(myParams)){
   column <-  which(names(myDf) == myParams[i])
   rowsOfInterest <- which(myDf[,column]==TRUE)
   curDf <- myDf[rowsOfInterest,]
   p <- p + geom_density(aes(x=curDf
$values),linetype=2,colour=myColors[i])
   cat(i,"\n")
   print(p)
}
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: Symbol Size in Legend Key
messages.body_plain:
Hi

At this time, it is impossible to directly specify the size (and the
other drawing parameters) of the geoms in legends.
As a dirty workaround, you can directly edit the grob objects using
grid editing function.

N = 10^3

a = seq(as.Date("1970-01-01"), by="day", length.out = N)
x = data.frame(date = a, x1 = 10/N*(1:N) + rnorm(N), x2 = 20/N*(1:N) +
rnorm(N))
x.m = melt(x, id.vars="date")
qplot(date, value,color=variable,data=x.m, size=I(1/2)) +
opts(legend.key.size = unit(c(1.2, 2.4), "lines"))

# edit the key.points
grid.gedit(size=unit(5, "mm"), "key.points", grep=T)

Probably the next version of ggplot2 will get this ability directly
specifying the appearance of legends.

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

messages.subject: Re: 2d error representation on scatterplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's my take:

w <- data.frame(value1 = c(2:5)+ rnorm(480),

                value2 = c(5:2)+rnorm(480),
                factor1 = as.factor(rep(1:4,120)),
                factor2 = as.factor(rep(rep(1:3,each=4),40)))
p <- ggplot(w, aes(value1, value2))
f <- facet_grid(factor1 ~ factor2)
p + f + geom_point()

p + f + geom_boxplot() + geom_point(colour = "red")

## Generate means and SDs for value1 and value2
summfun <- function(d) data.frame(v1mean = mean(d$value1), v1sd = sd(d$value1),
                                  v2mean = mean(d$value2), v2sd = sd(d$value2))
## Generate a data frame of such summaries for all factor combinations
wsumm <- ddply(w, .(factor1, factor2), summfun)

ggplot() + geom_point(data = w, aes(x = value1, y = value2)) +
    facet_grid(factor1 ~ factor2) +
    geom_errorbar(data = wsumm,
                  aes(x = v1mean, ymin = v2mean - v2sd, ymax = v2mean + v2sd),
                  color = 'red', size = 1, width = 0.2) +
    geom_errorbarh(data = wsumm,
                   aes(x = v1mean, y = v2mean, xmin = v1mean - v1sd,
xmax = v1mean + v1sd),
                   color = 'blue', size = 1, width = 0.2)

If you want CI bars, change the scale factor on x/ymin and x/ymax. Of
course, feel free to change the other arguments to your needs.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: north arrow and scale bar in ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: north arrow and scale bar in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
For anyone interested, here are two functions I wrote a while back to
simplify adding a very simple scalebar to a plot.

hscale_segment = function(breaks, ...)
{
    y = unique(breaks$y)
    stopifnot(length(y) == 1)
    dx = max(breaks$x) - min(breaks$x)
    dy = 1/30 * dx
    hscale = data.frame(ix=min(breaks$x), iy=y, jx=max(breaks$x),
jy=y)
    vticks = data.frame(ix=breaks$x, iy=(y - dy), jx=breaks$x, jy=(y +
dy))
    df = rbind(hscale, vticks)
    return(geom_segment(data=df,
                        aes(x=ix, xend=jx, y=iy, yend=jy),
                        ...))

}

hscale_text = function(breaks, ...)
{
    dx = max(breaks$x) - min(breaks$x)
    dy = 2/30 * dx
    breaks$y = breaks$y + dy
    return(geom_text(data=breaks,
                     aes(x=x, y=y, label=label),
                     hjust=0.5,
                     vjust=0,
                     ...))

}

Then it's a simple matter of defining the break points for the
scalebar and adding layers with the two above functions to your plot.
Defining the breaks obviously depends on your coordinate system, the
below example is for a projected metric coordinate system. (ymin,
xmax) is the lower right hand corner in which the scalebar is being
placed.

scalebreaks = data.frame(x=seq(xmax - 11000, xmax - 1000, 5000),
                         y=(ymin + 1000),
                         label=c("0", "5", "10 km"))

plot = (ggplot(...)
        + ...
        + hscale_segment(scalebreaks, size=0.1)
        + hscale_text(scalebreaks, size=2)
        + ...
        )

It will look about like this:

    0        5      10 km
    |--------|--------|

Adding a north arrow should be trivial, assuming you yourself know
which way north is.
