messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel- ( i should have sent this to the whole list the first time)

I believe the whole thing can be shortened to this.

## your data set

values <- runif(500,min=0,max=2)
param1 <- c(rep(TRUE,300),rep(FALSE,200))
param2 <- c(rep(TRUE,200),rep(FALSE,300))
param3 <- c(rep(TRUE,50),rep(FALSE,450))
myDf <- data.frame(values,param1,param2,param3)

## my code deviates here
m.myDf <- melt(myDf, id.vars='values')
m.myDf <- m.myDf[which(m.myDf$value),]
ggplot( m.myDf, aes(x=values,color=variable) ) + geom_density()

You, of course, could put this in a pdf. And if you want your specific colors, then scale_color_manual() can give you this.

The first thing to note is that overlaying as you were doing is the completely wrong paradigm with ggplot.

Looking at m.myDf you'll see it actually is looking a bit akward with "values" and "value". What's going on here is that myDf is melted against the variable "values": melt moves each param variable, while keeping its original "values" column lined up,  into the "value" column (the melt default variable name for the values) while also creating a "variable" column which describes which param it is (as a factor variable). All three params treated this way are then stacked row-wise, within these 3 columns.

Because your only computing the density on 'values' where 'value' of param is true, you can simply throw out wherever value==FALSE (ie keep which(value)). Then your data frame is already for ggplot.

A melted data frame is exactly what ggplot eats up. Learning to construct data frames and use melt is a huge part of using ggplot and worth the initial head scratching. I remember the first time I tried it. hehe. A rule of thumb, if it seems like too much code, it probably is.

~James

meltedDf <- meltedDf[meltedDf$value,]

#plot
p <- ggplot( meltedDf, aes(x=nsNormBySize,color=variable) ) +

p <- p + scale_x_continuous('Non-synonymous polymorphisms / CD

length',limits=c(0,0.01))

> 4: Removed 1158 rows containing missing values (stat_density).

This happens because of the limits you imposed on the x and y axis of
the graph. Apparently, the values of your remaining group lie outside
the imposed range. Here's a simple example to illustrate:

dd <- data.frame(x = rnorm(500))
ggplot(dd, aes(x = x)) + geom_density()
ggplot(dd, aes(x = x)) + geom_density() +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-2, 2))
Warning message:
Removed 17 rows containing missing values (stat_density).

The message informs you that 17 values were outside the interval -2 <=
x <= 2 that was used to generate the density estimate.
Your warning messages have a parallel interpretation.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
After fiddling 10 minutes with your data. I realized that this is because scale_continuous throws away data when using limits, as Dennis points out. You want to use coord_cartesian.

p <- ggplot( meltedDf, aes(x=nsNormBySize,color=variable) ) +

geom_density()

p <- p + scale_x_continuous('Non-synonymous polymorphisms / CD

length')

p <- p + scale_y_continuous('Density')

# next line causes error relating to length

p <- p + scale_colour_hue("Gene sets")

p + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.1), ylim = c(0, 350))

As to why the first level isn't plotted. Is being overploted by anyGO. See below

meltedDf2 <- meltedDf
meltedDf2$variable <- relevel(meltedDf2$variable, "anyGo")

p2 <- ggplot(meltedDf2, aes(x=nsNormBySize,color=variable) ) +
geom_density()

p2 <- p2 + scale_x_continuous('Non-synonymous polymorphisms / CD
length', breaks = seq(0, 0.01, 0.002))

p2 <- p2 + scale_y_continuous('Density')

# next line causes error relating to length

p2 <- p2 + scale_colour_hue("Gene sets")

p2 + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.01))

HTH

Luciano

dord<-ddply(d, .(l), f)
ggplot(aes(x=factor(l), y=v, fill=factor(a)),data=dord)+geom_bar()

messages.subject: interaction plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Does anyone happen to know of a short way to make interaction plots in
ggplot2?  Something along the order of:

d <- mtcars; xbar <- mean(d$wt); sdx <- sd(d$wt)
m <- lm(mpg ~ hp * wt, d)
d$x <- c(rep(range(d$hp), 3), rep(NA, 26))
d$y <- c(predict(m, data.frame(hp = rep(range(d$hp), 3),
  wt = rep(c(xbar - sdx, xbar, xbar + sdx), each = 2))),
  rep(NA, 26))
d$g <- c(rep(c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD"), each = 2), rep(NA, 26))

require(ggplot2)
ggplot(d, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = g))

#rm(d, xbar, sdx, m)

but preferably more automated.  I am not exactly wild about them, but
Psychology is tremendously fond of using these to break down
interactions so I find myself creating them quite frequently.  I know
there are some things like this that use base graphics (e.g., in
TeachingDemos) but I would prefer to stay in the pretty, flexible
environment of ggplot2.  If not I will hack something together.

Thanks,

Josh

--
Joshua Wiley
Ph.D. Student, Health Psychology
University of California, Los Angeles

messages.subject: Re: What's wrong with these geom_text and annotate(geom = "text") approaches?
messages.subject_clean: What's wrong with these geom_text and annotate(geom = "text") approaches?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bryan:

I always forget to use NULL (thanks for the reminder, Kohske :), but
part of the problem is that the x's and y's in the two data frames
used have different names. The error I got when running your code in
the console was

> p + geom_text(aes(label = grdlet, x = x, y = y), col = "red", data = z)

Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'freq' not found

where freq is defined as the y variable in the ggplot() call.

So I did a little rearranging :)  If I know I'm going to be using two
or more data frames to render a plot, I've learned to make the initial
ggplot() call as minimal as possible and pass the aesthetics to the
geoms, where they behave locally rather than globally. This way, the x
and y used in geom_linerange() don't clash with the x and y in
geom_text() because neither x nor y is assigned globally in the
ggplot() statement.

grdDist <- function(grd, shift = 0, ...) {
       cnt <- count(grd*100)

       p <- ggplot(data = cnt) +
              geom_linerange(aes(x = x, y = freq, ymin = 0, ymax =
freq), size = 2) +
              ylab("count") + xlab("grade") +

              geom_vline(xintercept = c(64.5, 69.5, 72.5, 76.5, 79.5,
                                        82.5, 86.5, 89.5, 93.5) + shift,
                                        col = "red", alpha = 0.2)

       # Now make a df with just the labeling info
       ym <- max(cnt$freq)*1.1
       z <- data.frame(grdlet = c("F", "D", "C-", "C", "C+", "B-",

                                  "B", "B+", "A-", "A"),

               x = c(62, 66, 71, 75, 77, 81, 85, 87, 91, 95) + shift, y = ym)
       print(z) # looks OK

       p <- p + geom_text(aes(label = grdlet, x = x, y = y), col =

"red", data = z)

       print(p)

       }

grd <- c(0.76, 0.83, 0.87, 0.88, 0.81, 0.87, 0.73, 0.89, 0.77, 0.81,
0.84, 0.83, 0.88, 0.83, 0.82, 0.84, 0.83, 0.86, 0.83, 0.76)

grdDist(grd)

You might want to play around with a couple of the x positions in the
text, but otherwise it looks OK to me.

HTH,
Dennis

This selection from Dennis' response is a great nugget of wisdom which
I'm sure will help me with several problems I've had!

Thanks as always.  Bryan

>
> If I know I'm going to be using two
> or more data frames to render a plot, I've learned to make the initial
> ggplot() call as minimal as possible and pass the aesthetics to the
> geoms, where they behave locally rather than globally. This way, the x
> and y used in geom_linerange() don't clash with the x and y in
> geom_text() because neither x nor y is assigned globally in the
> ggplot() statement.
>

Thanks for the solutions and explanations. I think I'm going to use
scale_x_log10() instead of coord_cartesian().

As far as I can tell, "Over-plotting" in ggplot can be deceiving. Not
sure how it could be better handled in future versions (perhaps
alternating colors to indicate multiple lines on the same coordinate?)
so the user is made aware of the situation.

Thanks,
Daniel

Daniel, I don't know if it would work. But you can try making the linetype an aesthetic so different linetypes are assigned and maybe you could see one behind the other. As for your I idea, I don't think the implementation would easy if possible because of the way graphics devices work. Each element of the plot is plotted once at a time and plotted over the earlier elements.

Luciano

messages.subject: Extract y-axis labels
messages.body_plain:
First of all, I'd like to state my appreciation for all the work
that's gone into ggplot2.

After trolling around lists for awhile, I've been unable to find an
answer to this question.

Suppose I have a figure generated by this code:

R> library(ggplot2)
R> df <- data.frame(x=1:100, y=1:100)
R> p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y))+ geom_point()

Is there a way to systematically extract the y-axis labels? In this
simple case, I'd like to extract 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. I have tried
looking through the output generated by:

R> str(p)

and was able to extract the y-axis title but not the labels.

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Edward

messages.subject: Re: interaction plots
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, May 20, 2011 at 3:51 AM, Brandon Hurr <brando...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I don't have one either, but if you do hack one together please share or
> feel free to let us help you hack.

Its a crude little thing for a very specific task, but since you asked
here it is:

IntPlot <- function(object, data, x, int, intvals, intnames,
                    mean = TRUE, n = 100, FUN = "glm", ...) {
  require(ggplot2)

  if (is.formula(object) && !missing(data)) {
    FUN <- match.fun(FUN)
    m <- FUN(formula = object, data = data, ...)
  ## likely not the best way to tell if there is a predict method
  } else if (is.data.frame(object$model) &&
    is.function(getS3method("predict", class(m)))) {
    m <- object
  } else stop("'object' must be a formula or an object with an appropriate
    method for 'predict' and a copy of the data")

  mdata <- m$model
  y <- as.character(formula(m)[[2]])

  vals <- as.data.frame(lapply(mdata, function(x) {
    if (is.numeric(x)) {
      if (mean) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) else 0
    } else {
      names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
    }}))

  if (missing(intvals)) {
    b <- c(mean(mdata[, int], na.rm = TRUE),
      sd(mdata[, int], na.rm = TRUE))
    intvals <- rep(c(b[1] - b[2], b[1], b[1] + b[2]), each = n)
    intnames <- c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")
  } else intvals <- rep(intvals, each = n)

  newdat <- do.call(rbind, rep(list(vals), length(intvals)))
  newdat[, int] <- intvals
  minx <- min(mdata[, x], na.rm = TRUE)
  maxx <- max(mdata[, x], na.rm = TRUE)
  rx <- seq(from = minx, to = maxx, length.out = n)

  newdat[, x] <- rep(rx, length(intvals)/n)

  preddat <- data.frame(predict(m, newdat, type = "response"),
    newdat[, x], factor(rep(intnames, each = n), levels = intnames))
  colnames(preddat) <- c(y, x, int)

  p <- ggplot(mdata, aes_string(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line(aes_string(x = x, y = y, colour = int), data = preddat)
  return(p)
}

## Examples of how I will use it (i.e., create a model or using an
existing model object)

m1 <- lm(mpg ~ hp * wt, mtcars)
m2 <- glm(vs ~ hp * wt, family = "binomial", data = mtcars)
IntPlot(cyl ~ hp * wt, mtcars, x = "wt", int = "hp")
IntPlot(cyl ~ hp * wt, mtcars, x = "wt", int = "hp", intvals = c(100,
300), intnames = c("low", "high"))
IntPlot(m1, x = "wt", int = "hp")
IntPlot(m2, x = "wt", int = "hp")

Josh

> Brandon

--
Joshua Wiley
Ph.D. Student, Health Psychology
University of California, Los Angeles
http://www.joshuawiley.com/

print(gplot, vp = vplot)

messages.subject: Re: flexible model fitting problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Colm,

I'm not sure exactly what you're looking for, but this is how I'd do it:

# Use ddply to create all the models/data at once
library(plyr)
library(MASS)
mods <- dlply(melted.d, "cl", function(df) {
  rlm(value ~ c + p, data = df)
})

n <- 10
grid <- with(d, expand.grid(
   c = seq(min(c), max(c), length = n),
   p = seq(min(p), max(p), length = n)
))

preds <- ldply(mods, function(model) {
  grid$value <- predict(model, newdata=grid)

  err <- predict(model, newdata=grid, se = TRUE)
  grid$ucl <- err$fit + 1.96 * err$se.fit
  grid$lcl <- err$fit - 1.96 * err$se.fit

  grid
})

ggplot(melted.d, aes(p, value)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = t, shape = t)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = lcl), data = preds, colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~ cl) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")

Hadley

messages.subject: bug in y-axis scaling for small values
messages.subject_clean: bug in y-axis scaling for small values
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I was quite puzzled to see an horizontal line in my graph today, until
I realised that it was a ggplot2 bug. The data were definitely not
constant, but small (around 1e-10 with some dispersion). Base plots
don't have any trouble finding the range of this data, and it's
clearly not a case of numerical accuracy either. Consider this minimal
example,

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
d1 <- d2 <- data.frame(x=seq(0,10, length=1e2),
                       y=rnorm(1e2, sd=1e-3))

d2$y <- d2$y * 1e-4

p1 <-
  ggplot(d1)+
  geom_path(aes(x,y))

# p1 is OK
p1

# p2 is displayed as a horizontal line
p1 %+% d2

with(d2, plot(x, y, t="l"))

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Getting a stacked barchard
messages.body_plain:
John,

Side-by-side bar charts make it difficult to see the pattern of changes in any one variable from month to month, as you have to visually "blank out" the intervening bars. Stacked bar charts have the advantage of showing the total (and I would guess that this is why the stacked version was requested), but make it almost impossible to see or interpret the changes in individual variables from month to month. Because both types of charts hide more data than they show, it's usually a good idea to avoid them. Stephen Few, Edward Tufte and William Cleveland have all written persuasively on the subject, and some of their materials can be found for free online.

Instead of bar charts, you might try line graphs with facets to separate the "a" and "b" groups in one of the panels. Line charts make it easy to compare values within and across groups and months. When you need to also show the combined total, the best approach is to stack a graph for total on top of a graph showing the individual values (this is something like Tufte's "small multiples"). In ggplot, this can be done using viewports.

Starting with your code (replacing "group" with "prodgroup" to avoid namespace conflicts, as pointed out by Dennis), the following produces something close to what I have in mind:

library(ggplot2, reshape2)
df1 <- structure(list(prod = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L,
3L), .Label = c("x",
"y", "z"), class = "factor"), jan = c(10L, 15L, 20L, 20L, 15L,
10L), feb = c(10L, 18L, 10L, 15L, 18L, 10L), march = c(10L, 10L,
34L, 17L, 34L, 18L), group = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L,
2L), .Label = c("a", "b"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("prod",

"jan", "feb", "march", "prodgroup"), class = "data.frame", row.names =
c(NA,
-6L))

df2 <- melt(df1,id= c("prod","prodgroup"))
str(df2)

# create a data frame containing the monthly total sales
m3 <- rowsum(df2$value, df2$variable)
df3 <- data.frame(variable = unique(df2$variable), value = m3)

# generate a line graph of individual sales, colored by product and grouped by "prodgroup"
ind.g <- ggplot() +
    facet_grid(facets = prodgroup ~ .) +
    geom_point(aes(x = variable,y = value,colour = prod),data=df2,alpha = 0.5952) +
    geom_line(aes(x = variable,y = value,colour = prod,group = prod),data=df2)
# generate a line graph of the total sales
sum.g <- ggplot() +
    geom_point(aes(x = variable,y = value),data=df3,alpha = 0.5952) +
    geom_line(aes(x = variable,y = value),data=df3)
# set up a device to plot multiple graphs
png("grid line chart.png", width = 800, height = 600)
grid.newpage()
# create two viewports, one above the other
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2,1)))
vplayout <- function(x, y)
    viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

# print total sales to the top viewport
print(sum.g, vp = vplayout(1,1))
# print individual sales to the bottom viewport
print(ind.g, vp = vplayout(2,1))
#close the device
dev.off()

Note that the above saves the graph as png in the current working directory; it does not display it within R.

With the above, there is a problem with alignment of the months between the top (total sales) panel and the bottom (individual product sales) panel. I can think of two ways to solve this display problem. One approach would be to control the width of the top viewport using the widths= argument. This seems like it would take some finessing to get right. A second approach would be to add the totals in df3 back into df2 using "prodgroup" = "total" and just plot a single graph using facets ("total," "a" and "b"), instead of the two graphs using viewports. Potential pitfalls of this approach are that you would need to control the order of facets using a third variable (as recently discussed in another thread on this discussion list) and that there might be insufficient visual distinction between the "total sales" graph and the other "individual" sales-by-group graphs.

Regards,

Tom

messages.subject: Re: Showing values in bar chart
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jüri,

I've ran in to the same issue myself. I've not found an easy way other than to create a second data set which contains the x and y position of the labels along with the text to print. For the example you have included I would do something like this:

library(ggplot2)
dplot <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, fill = cut)) +
    geom_bar(position = "fill")

# cross tabulate the two variables of interest
xt <- table(diamonds$cut, diamonds$clarity)
# turn counts in to column proportions
xt <- prop.table(xt, margin = 2)
# xt is the information we want to print, however we need to calculate
# where we want to print

# start by calculating the cumulative proportions (the tops of each of the bars)
cum.xt <- xt
for (m in 2:nrow(cum.xt)) {
    cum.xt[m, ] <- cum.xt[m-1, ] + cum.xt[m, ]
}

# calculate the midpoints in each of the bars, these will be the label positions
label.positions <- xt

for (m in 2:nrow(label.positions)) {
    label.positions[m, ] <- cum.xt[m-1, ] + xt[m, ] / 2
}

label.positions[1, ] <- label.positions[1,] / 2

# to keep things tidy collect all this information in to a data frame
xt <- melt(xt)
xt$value <- round(xt$value, 2)
label.positions <- melt(label.positions)

my.labels <- data.frame(x = xt$Var.2, y = label.positions$value,
    label = xt$value)

# finally, add the labels to dplot
dplot + geom_text(data = my.labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label))

# but as you can see there's not enough room for the categories
# with small proportions so let's remove them
my.labels <- subset(my.labels, label > 0.025)

# add a bit of transparency to the text and change the colour to white
# so it does not distract readers from the actual graphic
dplot + geom_text(data = my.labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    alpha = 0.6, colour = "white")

Cheers

Stu

messages.subject: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug
messages.subject_clean: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've discovered what I think is a bug in ggplot2's use of geom_text and am wondering if anyone out there has a work-around/is able to point out what I'm doing wrong.

Consider the following sample code:

library(ggplot2)

Treatment <- rep(c('C','T'),3)
Group <- rep(c('A','B','C'),each=2)
Response <- c(0.22894321, 0.23391813, 0.92256514, 0.92705167, 0.05982670, 0.09667674)
Differences <- c('+0pts',  '+0pts', '+0pts', '+0pts', '+4pts', '+4pts')

df <- data.frame(Treatment, Group, Response, Differences)

ydef <- c(0.03, 0.03, 0.2)

hist <- ggplot(df, aes(x=Group, y=Response, fill=Treatment, stat="identity"))
hist + geom_bar(position = "dodge")  + geom_text(aes(label = Differences,y=ydef))

If this works for you the same way that it does for me--using the most current versions of ggplot2 and R 2.12.2--groups B and C should have two text floats each, spaced equal distances apart. Obviously this is not what we want. Now change 'ydef' such that

ydef <- c(0.03, 0.03, 0.03)

re-run the script above, and the problem is solved--each group now only has one text float corresponding to differences (or rather two, layered exactly on top of each other). How does this make any sense? I've been using this basic structure in a fairly large scale application, and have not had any trouble until I got to this specific example with these specific numbers.

Part of the problem may be the way I'm constructing 'Differences', by adding it as a column to the data frame and placing this text on the chart with geom_text. If there was a way to do the same thing using a vector with only three character entries I'm sure that would solve the problem.

In short (1) help please! and (2) here is a potentially interesting bug for the consideration of the ggplot2 community.

Cheers,
Aaron

messages.subject: Re: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug
messages.subject_clean: Looking for help resolving a geom_text bug
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It's not really a bug but rather one of the nuances of ggplot2 that's
bitten you.

If you do this:

# Create a separate data frame for the text
df2 <- data.frame(Group = factor(LETTERS[1:3]),
                          ydef = c(0.03, 0.03, 0.20),
                          Differences = c('+0pts', '+0pts', '+4pts'),
                          stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# notice the classes and compare to df
str(df2)

# Modify the plot call:
hist <- ggplot(df)
hist + geom_bar(aes(x=Group, y=Response, fill=Treatment, stat="identity"),
                         position = 'dodge') +
      geom_text(data = df2, aes(x = Group, y = ydef, label = Differences))

It works as expected. The nuance is that the aesthetics you define in
ggplot() are expected to be present in every layer [geom]. It is often
the case that when geom_text() is one of the layers, you don't want
all the aesthetics (and all sets of values) in the original data
frame. In your case, the Treatment variable adds duplication to the
Differences. The 'solution' is to decouple the aesthetics needed in
the bar chart from those needed in the labels; one way to do that is
to create separate data frames for the two tasks, passing the
aesthetics information to the geoms rather than to ggplot() and
realizing that you can use different data frames in different layers.
[This is the nuance. :)]

By creating a separate data frame for the labels (x, y, label), you
can decouple the data used to produce the bar chart layer from that to
produce the text labels. When using different data sets in different
layers, you eventually learn (from getting your head beaten in by
ggplot2 :) to make the ggplot() statement as minimal as possible; this
is why you'll see examples where ggplot() is called without any
arguments and the data frames and aesthetics are passed to the
individual geoms. This also would have worked:

hist <- ggplot()
hist + geom_bar(data = df, aes(x=Group, y=Response, fill=Treatment,
stat="identity"),
                         position = 'dodge') +
      geom_text(data = df2, aes(x = Group, y = ydef, label = Differences))

Also notice I use the same variable name for x in each layer but
different y variables.

Admittedly, you don't see many examples of this in the on-line help,
but there are several such examples in the group archives, although
you may have to dig a bit to find them. This behavior isn't 'obvious',
but learning this little nugget about ggplot2 can be very beneficial
down the road.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: control lty-group assignment with legend
messages.body_plain:
The example below appears to demonstrate that ggplot2 will *only* automatically create a legend if the group variable identified in aes() is a factor or a character.

But in that case the user exercises no direct control over which lty is assigned to which group.

Below, I work an example where I assign lty=1 to women and lty=2 to men, but obtain no legend; and in another example I obtain a legend but am unable to specify what lty is assigned to what group.

Is there an elegant and simple way to remedy this?

set.seed(1)
junk<-data.frame(x=-3:2)
junk<-rbind(
 	cbind(junk, gender="F")
 		,
 	cbind(junk, gender="M")
)
junk$y<-junk$x^2 / 3 + rnorm(nrow(junk)) / 6
junk$gender_lty<-c(M=2, F=1)[as.character(junk$gender)]
print(junk)
require(ggplot2)
#	The following associates lty=2 with male and lty=1 with female,
#	but it creates no legend to enlighten the reader.
print(
 	ggplot(data=junk, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y, group=gender_lty, lty=gender_lty) )
 		+ geom_line()
)
#	This also creates no legend:
print(
 	ggplot(data=junk, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y, group=gender, lty=gender_lty) )
 		+ geom_line()
)
#	The following does create a legend, but I have no control over the
#	lty! Also, although factor() has associated the number 1 with women
#	and 2 with men, ggplot2 gives lty=3 to men. So the numeric values of
#	the factor have no bearing on which lty is given to which group.
print(
 	ggplot(data=junk, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y, group=gender, lty=gender) )
 		+ geom_line()
)
junk$whichNumberForWhichGender<-as.numeric(junk$gender)
print(junk)
# 	Finally, we observe the same behavior if the group variable is a
# 	character.
junk$chargender<-as.character(junk$gender)
print(str( junk$chargender))
print(
 	ggplot(data=junk, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y, group=chargender, lty=chargender) )
 		+ geom_line()
)

Thanks for any insight.

I really would like to decide which lty is assigned to which group, not allow a black box to make that decision it for me.

Jacob A. Wegelin
Assistant Professor
Department of Biostatistics
Virginia Commonwealth University
830 E. Main St., Seventh Floor
P. O. Box 980032
Richmond VA 23298-0032
U.S.A.

Hi

The linetype cannot process continuous value.
Though it wokrs at this time,
in the future version, if you use continuous value for lty, it will be error.

You can manually control the linetype like this:

ggplot(junk, aes(x, y, lty=gender)) + geom_line() +
scale_linetype_manual(values=c(5, 6), breaks=c("F", "M"))

--

The University of  Tokyo, Japan.

Thanks to all for their replies. Here is the example repeated with a simple and elegant solution thanks to Ista Zahn.

set.seed(1)
junk<-data.frame(x=-3:2)
junk<-rbind(
 	cbind(junk, gender="F")
 		,
 	cbind(junk, gender="M")
)
junk$y<-junk$x^2 / 3 + rnorm(nrow(junk)) / 6

print(junk)
require(ggplot2)
#	Suppose you are happy with the default linetypes and just want a
#	different title or name for the legend:
print(
 	ggplot(data=junk, aes(x=x, y=y, group=gender, linetype=gender))
 		+ geom_line()
 		+ scale_linetype(
 			name="Gender"
 		)
)
#	Suppose you want to personally exercise dominion over the linetype:
print(
 	ggplot(data=junk, aes(x=x, y=y, group=gender, linetype=gender))
 		+ geom_line()
 		+ scale_linetype_manual(
 			name="Gender"
 			, values=c(F=1, M=2)
 		)
)

messages.body_plain:
The example below creates a plot with a two-part legend.

I would like to place the legend at the top of the right margin, not halfway between the top and the bottom of that margin.

The "legend.justification" syntax does not return an error, but it does not seem to have any effect either.

Does documentation for "legend.justification" exist? It is briefly mentioned on page 112 of the ggplot2 book.

How would I locate the legend in the top right corner?

junk<-data.frame(
 	xaxis=seq(-3,3, length=30)
 	, gender="F"
)
junk2<-junk
junk2$gender<-"M"
junk<-rbind(junk , junk2)
rm(junk2)
junk$mu <- c(F=0.9, M=-1.3, A=1)[as.character(junk$gender)]
junk<-ddply(junk, .(gender), function( thispiece ){
 	thispiece$density<-dnorm( x=thispiece$xaxis, mean=thispiece[1,"mu"], sd=1)
 	thispiece
 	}
)
junk$observed <- c(F=-1.5, M=2, A=0.3)[as.character(junk$gender)]

require(ggplot2)
print(
 	ggplot(junk, aes(x=xaxis, y=density, group=gender, linetype=gender) )
 		+ geom_path()
 		+ geom_point( aes(x=observed, y=0.02, shape=gender), size=3)
 		+ scale_linetype_manual( name="Density", values=c(F=1, M=2))
 		+ scale_shape_manual( name="Observed", values=c(F=19, M=1))
 		+ scale_x_continuous(name="Possible values")
 		+ opts(
 			legend.direction = "vertical"
 			, legend.position = "right"
 			, legend.justification=c(0,0)

You need to adjust the legend.position and not the justification. It's kind of fiddly too. I tried using Inf (Infiinite) but that wasn't recognized. Perhaps there is a better way, but I do not know of it.

junk<-data.frame(
       xaxis=seq(-3,3, length=30)
       , gender="F"
)
junk2<-junk
junk2$gender<-"M"
junk<-rbind(junk , junk2)
rm(junk2)
junk$mu <- c(F=0.9, M=-1.3, A=1)[as.character(junk$gender)]
junk<-ddply(junk, .(gender), function( thispiece ){
       thispiece$density<-dnorm( x=thispiece$xaxis, mean=thispiece[1,"mu"], sd=1)
       thispiece
       }
)
junk$observed <- c(F=-1.5, M=2, A=0.3)[as.character(junk$gender)]

require(ggplot2)
print(
       ggplot(junk, aes(x=xaxis, y=density, group=gender, linetype=gender) )
               + geom_path()
               + geom_point( aes(x=observed, y=0.02, shape=gender), size=3)
               + scale_linetype_manual( name="Density", values=c(F=1, M=2))
               + scale_shape_manual( name="Observed", values=c(F=19, M=1))
               + scale_x_continuous(name="Possible values")
               + opts(
                       legend.direction = "vertical"

                       , legend.position = c(0.8,0.7)
                       , legend.justification=c(0,0)
       )
)

messages.subject: Error with geom_ribbon and scale_x_continuous?
messages.body_plain:
I'm using geom_ribbon to create a confidence interval and I wanted to
zoom in on the graph.  After adding the scale_x_continuous function,
large chunks of the ribbon also got removed.

x=seq(0,1,length=100)
data <- data.frame(x=x, ymin=x-.1, ymax=x+.1)

# Ribbon exists on x-values between 0 and 1
ggplot(data, aes(x=x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax))

# I expect the ribbon to exist on x-values between 0.6 and 1
# but it only shows up for 0.7 to 0.9... corresponding to the major
grid lines
ggplot(data, aes(x=x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=ymin, ymax=ymax)) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits=c(.6,1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits=c(.6,1))

This can easily be worked around by just removing the appropriate rows
of my data.frame, but figured it was worth learning why this isn't a
bug, or making the bug known.

Thanks,

Derek

resolution) in an earlier thread:

Everyone else seems to comment on the fact that the axis title text is
very close to the tick mark labels, but to my eye the axis title is
positioned correctly, but the tick mark labels are spaced further away
from the tick marks. (cf compare the OP's theme_bw vs theme_gray
plots). When I've encountered this in my plots, my main issue is that
in theme_bw(), axis.text.x seems unresponsive to setting vjust; their
spacing relative to the tick marks remains the same for vjust set to
0, 0.5 or 1.

messages.subject: Error: attempt to apply non-function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

below an example of a qplot failure when seq is the name of a variable
in the calling environment. I would consider this a nuisance, maybe
even a bug. Maybe it is related to the use of parent.frame() in
qqplot?

Cheers,
Jochen

library(ggplot2)
x <- -10:10
y <- sin(x)
s <- data.frame(x=x, y=y)
qplot(x=x, y=y, data=s)
# works

seq <- s
qplot(x=x, y=y, data=s)
# Error in get(x, envir = this, inherits = inh)(this, ...) :
#  attempt to apply non-function

rm(seq)
qplot(x=x, y=y, data=s)
# works again
